lessons.intro: French writes letters it never says. Not a few odd ones: most final consonants, every H, and the final -E all sit on the page in silence. This lesson gives you one default and four overrides, so that any French word you have never seen before, on a menu, a street sign, a train ticket, comes out of your mouth close to right on the first try.

ipa.body: Sounds appear two ways in this course. IPA sits between slashes and is exact, the same alphabet linguists use worldwide: /pə.ti/. The respelling sits between brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [pə-TEE]. When the two disagree, trust the IPA. A small raised n, as in [GRAHⁿ], marks a nasal vowel: it means the vowel is sent through the nose, NOT that you should say an N.
ipa.title: The two notations, and what each is for

hMuet.body: Muet means mute. No H is ever pronounced in French, so this is not about sound at all: it is about grammar. An H muet behaves as though the letter were simply not there, so the word in front of it elides in the normal way. Le plus homme becomes l'homme, exactly as le plus arbre becomes l'arbre. Most French H words are muet.
hMuet.title: H muet: the H that lets the article shrink

examples.note: l'homme
l'hôtel
l'heure

careful.body: Most final consonants in French are silent. Four of them usually are not: C, R, F and L. Spell those four out and you get the English word CaReFuL, which is the whole point of the name: it is a memory hook, not a French word. When you reach the end of a word you have never seen, ask one question. Is the last letter C, R, F or L? If yes, say it. If no, stay quiet. That single question gets you most of the way, every time, and the rest of this lesson is the handful of cases where it needs help.
careful.title: CaReFuL: the four letters that stay awake

examples.note: C sounded
R sounded
F sounded
L sounded

eSwitch.body: A final -e is itself silent. It is never a syllable, so porte is one sound, PORT, and never POR-tuh. What it does is wake the consonant standing in front of it. grand ends on a nasal vowel with a silent D; add the -e and grande releases a real D at the end. This is why French gender is audible: a hard consonant at the end of an adjective usually means there is an -e behind it, which usually means feminine. Your ears can do grammar.
eSwitch.title: The final -e: an alarm clock for the letter before it

examples.note: masculine, D silent
feminine, D wakes
one syllable, not two

hAspire.body: Aspiré means breathed, and the name is misleading: an H aspiré is NOT breathed and makes no sound, exactly like an H muet. The only difference is grammatical. An H aspiré blocks the elision, so the article stays whole: le héros, not l'héros. There is no way to hear which kind an H is from the word alone. You learn it with the article, the same way you learn a noun with its gender.
hAspire.title: H aspiré: the H that blocks elision

examples.note: le héros, no elision
le hibou
le haricot

liaison.body: These silent finals are sleeping, not dead. When the next word begins with a vowel, some of them come back and link across the gap: deux euros is said /dø.zø.ʁo/, with the X of deux returning as a Z. That linking is called liaison, and it is the whole of your next lesson. For now it is enough to know why French bothers writing letters it does not say: because sometimes it does say them.
liaison.title: Liaison: when a silent letter wakes up

examples.note: the Z here is a liaison

erEnding.body: CaReFuL says an R at the end of a word should sound. That is right about half the time, and wrong on every verb in the language. The reason is that -er is not a word ending, it is a GRAMMATICAL ending: it marks an infinitive (parler, manger, to speak, to eat) or a job noun (boulanger, a baker). Grammatical endings follow their own rule, and this one is pronounced as a single /e/ with the R completely silent. Short standalone words like hiver and mer are not carrying an ending at all, so their R stays alive.
erEnding.title: The -er ending: where CaReFuL stops applying

examples.note: infinitive, R silent
job noun, R silent
short word, R sounded
short word, R sounded

silentEnt.body: Four letters, two completely different jobs. On a conjugated verb, -ent is entirely silent: ils parlent is /il paʁl/ and sounds exactly like il parle. On a noun or an adverb it is a real nasal vowel: vent, content and comment all end in /ɑ̃/. There is one question that separates them. Is this a conjugated verb? If yes, the ending is silent. If no, you hear it.
silentEnt.title: The -ent ending: silent on a verb, sounded on anything else

verb, -ent silent

contains: the oddities: héroïne, onze, oui, yaourt, huit

sections.body: No H is ever pronounced in French. The two kinds differ in one thing only: whether the word in front of them elides. H muet takes l' and links; H aspiré keeps le or la and blocks the link.
sections.title: The only difference that matters
H aspiré: keeps le or la

sections.body: héros is aspiré but héroïne is muet, which is genuinely irregular. onze, oui, yaourt and huit behave like aspiré words without having an H at all: le onze, le yaourt, le huit.
sections.title: The oddities

sheets.title: Why French writes what it does not say
contains: why silent letters still have jobs

sections.body: Old French said most of these letters. Between roughly the 12th and 16th centuries the endings stopped being pronounced, and the spelling did not follow, partly because printers had already fixed it and partly because scholars deliberately kept the Latin shape visible. temps keeps its P and S from Latin tempus. doigt gained its G from digitus centuries after anyone said it.
sections.title: They used to be pronounced

sections.body: A silent letter is not decoration. It separates homophones on the page, marks gender and number that the ear cannot hear, and wakes up in liaison before a vowel. Remove the S from les amis and you lose the plural entirely.
sections.title: What they still do
Homophone sets the spelling keeps apart

sheets.title: How to read the sounds in this course

sections.body: IPA sits in slashes and is exact: /pə.ti/. The respelling sits in brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [pə-TEE]. When they disagree, the IPA is right.
sections.title: Two notations, two jobs

sections.body: A nasal vowel is one sound made through the nose. It is not a vowel plus an N. Writing [GRAHN] tells you to close your mouth on a consonant that French never says, which is the exact error this lesson exists to remove, so the superscript marks the nasality without ever spelling a consonant.
sections.title: Why the superscript matters

rows: from the throat, never the tongue tip

overview.introFr: En français, beaucoup de lettres s'écrivent mais ne se prononcent pas. Ce sont surtout les consonnes finales, le H et le -E final. Dans cette leçon, vous apprenez une règle par défaut et quatre exceptions.

goals.s: Read petit, grand, beaucoup, Paris and trop aloud without adding a single sound French does not make.
Sound the C, R, F and L that stay awake at the end of a word: sac, hiver, chef, avril.
Say parler and boulanger with a silent R, while keeping the R alive in hiver and mer.
Start l'hôtel and l'homme straight on the vowel, and know why le héros keeps its full article.
Tell grand from grande and petit from petite by ear alone, with no other clue in the sentence.
Say ils parlent so it sounds exactly like je parle, because it does.
Meet a French word you have never seen, on a menu or a sign, and get its ending right on the first attempt.

sections.intro: Your eyes see the last letter and your mouth starts loading it before you have decided anything. That happens in about a fifth of a second, which is faster than any rule you can consciously apply. So the rule has to become a reflex, and reflexes are built by doing, not reading.

closing.text: Do the finger stop on the first three French words you see tomorrow, on any sign or label. Silent unless there's a reason. Thirty seconds a day beats an hour once.

targets.sub: For any word ending in a default-silent letter
targets.label: The finger stop
steps: Read the word silently, all the way to the end.
Put a finger over the final letter so you cannot see it.
Say only what is left on the page.
Take the finger away and say it again exactly the same way. Do not let the letter back in.
Repeat until step four sounds like step three with no effort.

targets.sub: For words that must end open
targets.label: The vowel landing
steps: Say the word and hold the last sound for two full seconds.
If you can hold it, it is a vowel and you are correct.
If it stops dead, you closed on a consonant that should not be there.
Try again and land on the vowel like a step you are settling onto, not a door you are shutting.

targets.sub: For the masculine and feminine pair
targets.label: The switch check
steps: Say the masculine form. It should end open, on a vowel.
Now say the feminine. Release the woken consonant cleanly and stop.
Do not add a small uh after it. The -e is silent, it is only the switch.
Alternate the pair six times without pausing between them.

say.text: Every French teacher hears these eight, every week, from every English speaker. None of them are careless. Each one is a good instinct pointed at the wrong language.

errors.why: English says nearly every letter it writes. Cat ends in a real T. Your reading reflex was built on a language where the last letter is a promise, and French breaks that promise on most words.
errors.right: petit /pə.ti/ [pə-TEE]
errors.wrong: petit said as [pə-TEET]

errors.why: A final P is unusual enough in English that when you see one you make sure to pronounce it. That extra care is exactly what gives you away here.
errors.right: beaucoup /bo.ku/ [boh-KOO]
errors.wrong: beaucoup said as [boh-KOOP]

errors.why: You learned CaReFuL and applied it faithfully. The problem is that -er is a grammatical ending, not a word ending, and endings follow their own rule. Being consistent is what led you astray.
errors.right: parler /paʁ.le/ [par-LAY]
errors.wrong: parler said as [par-LEHR]

errors.why: This is over-correction, and it usually shows up in week three. You learned that French drops final consonants and started dropping all of them. The default is strong, not absolute.
errors.right: sac /sak/ [SAK]
errors.wrong: sac said as [SA]

errors.why: English H is a real sound and it is at the front of the word, where your mouth commits before you have thought. You are not adding a letter, you are failing to remove a habit.
errors.right: l'hôtel /lo.tɛl/ [lo-TEL]
errors.wrong: hôtel said with a breath, [HO-tel]

errors.why: You have heard French sung, or heard southern French, where the final -e does get a small vowel. It is real, it is just not standard spoken French, and it adds a syllable that changes the rhythm of the whole sentence.
errors.right: porte /pɔʁt/ [PORT]
errors.wrong: porte said as [POR-tuh]

errors.why: You met -ent in comment and vent, where it genuinely is a nasal /ɑ̃/. Then you met it on a verb and applied what you already knew. Same four letters, two completely different jobs.
errors.right: ils parlent /il paʁl/ [eel PARL]
errors.wrong: ils parlent said as [eel par-LAHⁿ]

errors.why: You applied the silent-S default correctly and got a real French word, just the wrong one. fil is thread. This is one of about six words you simply have to bank, and the rules will not save you.
errors.right: fils /fis/ [FEES]
errors.wrong: fils said as [FEEL]

sections.body: An hour ago the ending of a French word was a coin toss. Now you have a default, four overrides and a short list of stubborn words. That is the entire system, and the rest of French pronunciation builds directly on top of it. The R was the hard one and you have been through it twice, from both ends: producing it in the trap drill, hearing it in the listening drill.

say.text: Last round. The letter that wakes others up, and the handful of words that ignore everything you have learned.

questions.q: What does a silent final -e do to the consonant before it?
questions.why: grand /ɡʁɑ̃/ becomes grande /ɡʁɑ̃d/. The E stays silent and the D starts sounding.

questions.q: You hear a clear T at the end of an adjective. It is probably:
questions.why: A sounded final consonant usually means an -e woke it, and that -e is the feminine marker. Your ears can do grammar.

questions.q: Which pair sounds IDENTICAL?
questions.why: The plural -s is silent, so the noun does not change. Only the article carries the number.

questions.q: Tap the letters you do not say.
questions.why: /il paʁl/. All four letters of -ent go silent on a conjugated verb. Stop after the L.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: A /z/ at the end. The final -e woke the S, and a woken S between vowels comes out as /z/.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: fils /fis/ ends in an S sound, which the default says should not happen. It is one of about six words you memorise.

questions.q: A learner says [PAR-lahⁿ] for « ils parlent ». Fix it.
questions.why: They borrowed the /ɑ̃/ from comment and vent, where -ent really is nasal. On a verb, all four letters are silent.

questions.q: Say it: « Elle est grande. »
questions.why: Release the D and stop. No small uh after it: the -e is a switch, not a syllable.

say.text: That is the lesson. Six things worth keeping, and the last one is where you go next.

sections.body: An hour ago you sounded the x in deux and a woman in a bakery could not understand you. The fix was not a longer list of words. It was one default and four overrides, and you now run them without thinking about most of them. From here, every new French word you meet has a first guess attached to it before you even try to say it. That is the difference between reading French and decoding it.
sections.title: What you take with you
points: Silent unless there's a reason. That is your default for every final consonant, on every word, forever.
CaReFuL: C, R, F, L are the reason, most of the time. sac, hiver, chef, avril.
The -er ending overrules CaReFuL. parler and boulanger drop the R. hiver and mer keep it.
H is a ghost. Never a sound. It only decides whether the article shrinks: l'homme against le héros.
A silent final -e is an alarm clock for the consonant in front of it, and that is how you hear gender.
Those silent finals are sleeping, not dead. Before a vowel, some of them wake up: deux‿euros, petit‿ami. That is liaison, and it is your next lesson.

errorTriggers.description: Sounds a final consonant that should be silent: the T in petit, the P in beaucoup, the S in Paris, the X in deux.
Drops a CaReFuL final that should sound (sac becomes /sa/), or over-applies CaReFuL to the -er ending (parler becomes /paʁ.lɛʁ/).
Breathes the H, or mixes up muet and aspiré: elides before héros, blocks elision before homme.
Pronounces a final -e as its own syllable (porte becomes /pɔʁ.tə/), or fails to sound the consonant it wakes (grande stays /ɡʁɑ̃/).
Applies a rule to one of the memorised exceptions: says /fil/ for fils, /tu/ for the pronoun tous, /nɛ/ for net.

recorded.desc: The station break beat: « ou » read flat as an English reader writes it, then « où » in the agent's own delivery. Both must be acoustically identical, which is the point of the beat.
café, été, école, métro, télé, clé, thé, santé, idée, désolé, préféré, cinéma, étudiant. Isolated, 900ms gaps, the é clearly /e/ with no glide onto an English AY diphthong.

père, mère, frère, très, après, élève, chèvre, bière, première, collège, sincère. Isolated, 900ms gaps, the è audibly wider than the é set above. Record back to back with rec-aigu-nine in one session so the contrast is real.
fête, tête, forêt, hôpital, être, château, île, goût. Isolated, 900ms gaps. No trace of an s anywhere, which learners expect to hear once told the mark replaced one.
des/dès, métro/mètre, mais/maïs, a/à, ou/où, sur/sûr. Each pair twice: separately, then back to back with a 400ms gap. The last three pairs must be indistinguishable, and that is the take to keep.
a/à, ou/où, sur/sûr, gâteau. The three pairs must be identical takes in every measurable way. If the two halves differ the recording teaches the opposite of the mission.
mais, maïs, Noël, naïf, égoïste, Haïti. The split syllables audibly separated with a light glottal break, so ma-EESS never collapses into MEH.
français, garçon, ça, leçon, reçu, déçu, carte, ceci. The first six on a clean /s/, carte on a hard /k/ and ceci on a soft c with no tail, so the whole contrast is on one tape.

lessons.intro: French writes five marks over its letters, and none of them is decoration. Two change which vowel comes out of your mouth, one splits a syllable in two, one changes a consonant, and several change nothing you can hear at all while still deciding which word you have written. This lesson gives you the one question that sorts them, so a marked word you have never seen comes out close to right on the first try.

ipa.body: Sounds appear two ways in this course. IPA sits between slashes and is exact, the same alphabet linguists use worldwide: /ka.fe/. The respelling sits between brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [ka-FAY]. When the two disagree, trust the IPA. A small raised n, as in [frahⁿ-SEH], marks a nasal vowel: the vowel is sent through the nose, and it does NOT mean you should say an N.
ipa.title: The two notations, and what each is for

trema.body: Two dots, and the only French mark that is an instruction about SYLLABLES rather than about a sound. French normally fuses neighbouring vowels into one sound: ai is a single /ɛ/, oi is a single /wa/. A tréma on the second vowel cancels that and forces both to be said separately. mais is one syllable, MEH. maïs is two, ma-EESS, and it means corn rather than but. The dots are the entire difference between those two words, on the page and in the mouth.
trema.title: The tréma: two dots that pull two vowels apart

examples.note: maïs, two syllables
mais, one syllable
Noël, noh-EL

cedille.body: The hook under a c, and the only mark in this lesson that goes on a consonant. French c follows the same rule English c does: before e or i it is soft, an /s/, and before a, o or u it is hard, a /k/. The cédille overrides that. It appears only before a, o or u, and it forces the soft /s/ where a /k/ would otherwise be. That is why it is never needed before e or i, where the c is already soft: a word like ceci has no tail because it does not need one. Without the tail, français would be read frankay and garçon would be gar-KOHN.
cedille.title: The cédille: the tail that keeps a C soft

examples.note: français, soft c before a
garçon, soft c before o
carte, no tail, hard c

accentAigu.body: The rising stroke, and the one you will meet most. It appears on the letter e and on no other letter in the language, which makes it the easiest mark to read: é is always the same sound, /e/, the vowel in the English word day with no glide at the end. It is on the past participle of every regular verb in French, so you will see it in almost every sentence you ever read. When you meet an é, you do not have to work anything out. Say AY.
accentAigu.title: The accent aigu: the mark that only ever goes on an e

examples.note: café, the final vowel sounds
two marks, one sound, twice
three é in one word

accentGrave.body: The falling stroke, and the one mark in French that does two unrelated things depending on which letter it sits on. On an e it changes the sound: è is /ɛ/, the vowel in the English word bed, wider and flatter than é. On an a or a u it changes nothing you can hear at all: à sounds exactly like a, and où sounds exactly like ou. There it is doing grammar rather than sound, separating two words that would otherwise be spelled identically. So the question to ask is not what the mark is, it is which letter it is on.
accentGrave.title: The accent grave: two completely different jobs

examples.note: père, the è is /ɛ/
où, same sound as ou
à, same sound as a

circonflexe.body: The little hat, and the most useful mark on the page for an English reader, because it is usually a receipt. Where French now writes a circumflex, the word almost always used to carry an s that has since dropped out, and English very often borrowed the word while the s was still there. So hôpital is hospital, forêt is forest, fête is feast, île is isle. Cover the hat, imagine an s after the vowel, and you can often read a word you have never seen. On an e it also opens the vowel to /ɛ/, the same sound as è. On an a, i, o or u it makes no difference a beginner needs to hear.
circonflexe.title: The circumflex: a receipt for a letter that left

examples.note: hôpital, hospital
forêt, forest
île, isle

minimalPair.body: Two words spelled identically except for one thing, where that one thing changes the meaning. They are the sharpest tool for learning a mark, because they remove every other clue: if ou and où are different words, the mark is carrying the difference by itself and nothing else can be doing it. This lesson uses five of them. Two of the pairs sound identical and are told apart only on the page, and three of them sound genuinely different, which is the distinction worth holding on to.
minimalPair.title: A minimal pair: two words, one difference

examples.note: des, DAY
dès, DEH

sections.say: There are two kinds, and they fail in different ways.
sections.body: Some pairs sound identical and are told apart only on the page: a and à, ou and où, sur and sûr. Getting those wrong is a writing error, and no amount of listening will help you. Other pairs genuinely differ in sound: des and dès, métro and mètre, mais and maïs. Getting those wrong is a speaking error, and the fix is your ear. Knowing which kind you are looking at tells you which skill to use.

sections.say: This is the single most useful reading trick in the lesson.
sections.body: French dropped an s from a large number of words between the eleventh and eighteenth centuries and marked the gap with a circumflex. English borrowed many of those same words from French BEFORE the s left, and kept it. So the hat is frequently a pointer at an English word you already know. Cover the mark, imagine an s directly after the vowel, and read what you get.
sections.title: Why the hat is a gift to an English reader

sections.say: It is a strong pattern, not a law.
sections.body: Some circumflexes mark a lost vowel rather than a lost s (âge was aage), and some simply distinguish two words (sûr from sur, dû from du). être has no s in its history at all. Try the s first, because it works far more often than not, and drop it when the result is not a word.

sections.say: When the two disagree, trust the IPA.
sections.body: Sounds appear two ways in this course. IPA sits between slashes and is exact, the same alphabet linguists use worldwide: /ka.fe/. The respelling sits between brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [ka-FAY]. When the two disagree, trust the IPA. A small raised n, as in [frahⁿ-SEH], marks a nasal vowel: the vowel is sent through the nose, and it does NOT mean you should say an N.

goals.s: Read café, été and désolé with a clean /e/, the vowel in day, and no glide on the end of it.
Tell des from dès and métro from mètre by ear alone, with nothing else in the sentence to help.
Meet hôpital and forêt cold, put the missing s back, and recognise the English word underneath.
Say maïs as two syllables and mais as one, and know which of them means corn.
Say français and garçon with a soft c, and explain why ceci never needs the tail.
Say à, ou and sur without hunting for a sound that is not there, because some marks change nothing you can hear.

cards.body: That is the whole lesson in one line. In English a mark is a flourish you can drop when typing. In French it is a letter, and dropping it can give you a different word.

cards.body: The names are useful later. What you need at reading speed is one question: does this mark change the vowel, the syllable, the consonant, or nothing at all? Four answers, and every mark in French is one of them.

say.text: Six mistakes, each one common enough that you will make at least two of them this week.

errors.why: Leaving the mark off is not a typing shortcut. The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it, and a French reader sees a misspelling exactly as you would see cafe written cofe.
errors.right: café, école, étudiant
errors.wrong: writing cafe, ecole, etudiant

errors.why: é is narrow, the vowel in day with no glide. è is wide and flat, the vowel in bed. des and dès are different words and this is the only thing separating them.
errors.right: /e/ for é, /ɛ/ for è
errors.wrong: reading é and è as the same vowel

errors.why: The circumflex marks where the s used to be, so the s is gone from the mouth as well as the page. Put it back to recognise the word, never to pronounce it.
errors.right: /o.pi.tal/, oh-pee-TAL
errors.wrong: saying an English hospital for hôpital

errors.why: The tréma is an instruction about syllables. It cancels the fusion of ai, which is why maïs is corn and mais is but.
errors.right: ma-EESS, two syllables
errors.wrong: reading maïs as one syllable

errors.why: Without the tail the c sits before a or o, where French c is a hard /k/. You would be saying gar-KOHN and frankay.
errors.right: garçon, français
errors.wrong: garcon, francais

errors.why: Some marks change nothing you can hear. On an a or a u the grave separates two words on the page, and listening harder will never reveal a difference that is not there.
errors.right: they are identical to a and ou
errors.wrong: hunting for a sound in à and où

opts: the word is borrowed from English
an s used to sit after the vowel

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a lost-s circumflex?
questions.why: être is simply spelled that way and has no English cousin with an s. hospital, forest and feast all kept theirs, which is what makes the trick worth trying first.

questions.q: You hear /de/. Which word is it?
questions.why: des is /de/, the narrow vowel, and it means some. dès is /dɛ/, wide, and it means from. Here the grave really does change the sound.

questions.q: Spot the error: « Je prends le mètro. »
questions.why: The underground is métro, with an é: /me.tʁo/. mètre with a grave is the unit of length, /mɛtʁ/. One mark apart, two unrelated words.

say.text: Round two. The marks that change nothing in the mouth.

questions.q: How does « où » sound compared to « ou »?
questions.why: Identical. The grave on a u changes nothing you can hear: it exists only to separate where from or on the page.
opts: with a w at the front

questions.q: Il ___ trente ans.
questions.why: a with no mark is the verb, he has. à with the grave is the preposition, to or at. They sound the same, so only the grammar chooses.

questions.q: Je vais ___ Paris.
questions.why: Going TO somewhere takes à. The bare a is the verb form of avoir, which would make this sentence say I go has Paris.

questions.q: What is the difference between « sur » and « sûr » when spoken?
questions.why: Nothing. Both are /syʁ/. The hat marks the s that dropped out of the old spelling, and it separates on from sure on the page only.

questions.q: Type the word that means where.
questions.why: où, with the grave. It is the only French word that uses a grave on a u, and writing ou instead gives you the word for or.

questions.q: If two spellings sound identical, the mark is:
questions.why: It is doing grammar. The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it. Leaving it off does not write the word less carefully, it writes a different word.

questions.q: Say the pair: « sur, sûr ».
questions.why: Both halves must come out identical. Any audible difference means you are inventing a sound the mark does not make.

questions.q: Which mark does « gâteau » carry, and what does it change?
questions.why: A circumflex on an a. It marks a lost s, and most speakers make no audible difference at all. A cédille never goes on a g, and there is no tréma here.
opts: a grave, and it changes the vowel
a circumflex, and it changes almost nothing
a tréma, and it splits the vowels
a cédille, and it softens the g

say.text: Round three. Two dots, and what they do to a syllable.

questions.q: How many syllables in « maïs »?
questions.why: Two: ma-EESS. The tréma cancels the fusion of ai into a single sound, which is the whole reason the dots are there.

questions.q: How many syllables in « mais »?
questions.why: One: /mɛ/. With no dots, ai behaves normally and fuses into a single vowel. This is the word that means but.

questions.q: What is a tréma an instruction about?
questions.why: Syllable count. Every other mark in this lesson is about a sound or about telling words apart. The tréma alone is about how many vowels you actually say.

questions.q: How is « Noël » said?
questions.why: Two syllables, noh-EL. Without the dots the oe would fuse, which is exactly what the tréma is there to prevent.

questions.q: Type the French word for corn.
questions.why: maïs, with the dots on the i. Spelling it mais gives you the word for but, and drops the word to one syllable.

questions.q: Which word carries a tréma?
questions.why: égoïste, on the i: ay-goh-EEST. It carries two marks doing two different jobs, since the é makes a sound and the ï splits one.

questions.q: Say it: « maïs ».
questions.why: Two clean syllables with a break between them. If it comes out as one, you have said but rather than corn.

questions.q: Tap the letters in « Noël » that carry a mark.
questions.why: Only the ë. The two dots sit on the e and force it into its own syllable, away from the o in front of it.

say.text: Round four. The only mark in the lesson that is not on a vowel.

questions.q: What does the cédille do in « français »?
questions.why: It forces the soft /s/. The c sits before an a, where a bare c would be /k/, so without the tail the word would open frankay.
opts: makes the c a soft s
makes the c a hard k

questions.q: Before which letters can a cédille appear?
questions.why: a, o and u, the three that make a c hard. Before e or i the c is already soft, so the tail would have nothing to do.

questions.q: Why does « ceci » never take a cédille?
questions.why: c before e or i is soft with no help. The cédille exists only to override a HARD c, and there is no hard c here to override.
opts: the c is already soft before e
the cédille only goes on capitals

questions.q: How would « garcon », written without the tail, be read?
questions.why: gar-KOHⁿ. The c sits before an o, so with no cédille it is a hard /k/. The tail is what makes the word sound like the one you say to a waiter.

questions.q: Type the French word for boy.
questions.why: garçon, with the tail under the c. Writing garcon changes the consonant, not just the look of it.

questions.q: Which word does NOT need a cédille?
questions.why: ceci. Its c comes before an e, so it is soft already. The other three all have a c before a or o and would go hard without the tail.

questions.q: Spot the error: « Je parle francais. »
questions.why: The c needs its tail before the a. Without it the word reads frankay, which is not a word in any language.

questions.q: Say it: « Je parle français ».
questions.why: The last word must land on a soft /s/ and a wide /ɛ/. A hard k anywhere in it means the cédille did not reach your mouth.

say.text: One idea and four rules. That is the whole lesson.

sections.body: The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it. Every mark in French is answering one of four questions: does it change the vowel, the syllable, the consonant, or nothing at all? You now have all four answers, which means you can read a marked word you have never seen and get it close to right on the first attempt.
sections.title: What you take with you
points: é is /e/, always. è and ê are /ɛ/, wider and flatter.
A circumflex usually marks a lost s, so put one back and look for the English word.
A tréma splits two vowels into two syllables: maïs is corn, mais is but.
A cédille keeps a c soft before a, o or u, and is never needed before e or i.

segments.text: I am Liam, and this lesson is the five accent marks French uses, and what each one actually changes.
Here is the idea the whole lesson hangs on. The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it.
café
That mark is not a flourish on the e. It is the reason you hear the last syllable at all.
Four questions cover every mark in the language. Does it change the vowel, the syllable, the consonant, or nothing at all?
Start with the vowel. The rising stroke, on an e, is always the same sound.
été
Two marks, one sound, twice. Now the falling stroke, which is wider and flatter.
père
Listen to the two of them side by side. Narrow first, then wide.
métro
mètre
One mark apart, and two unrelated words: the underground, and the unit of length.
The hat is different again. It usually marks an s that dropped out, and English often kept it.
hôpital
Cover the hat, put an s back, and there is your English word.
Your turn. Say each one after me.
Two dots next. They are not about a sound, they are about how many syllables you say.
maïs
Now without me. How do you say the word for boy, with the tail under the c?
And the word for school.
One more. The word for Christmas, and remember it is two syllables.
Two checks. First, one of these two sounds different from the other. Say the one that means from, rather than some.
Now the harder kind. These two sound identical, so say the one that means where.
Four rules worth keeping. é is narrow, è and ê are wide.
A hat usually means a lost s, so put one back and look for the English word.
Two dots mean two syllables. A tail under a c keeps it soft before a, o or u.
And when a mark changes nothing you can hear, it is still doing a job. The mark is part of the letter, not decoration on it.
À bientôt.

errorTriggers.description: Reads é and è as the same vowel, or ignores the mark entirely: says /kaf/ for café, /me.tʁo/ for mètre.
Hunts for a sound in à, où or sûr that is not there, or writes a where à is needed because they sound alike.
Fuses a tréma vowel into one syllable: reads maïs as mais, or Noël as a single sound.
Drops the cédille and hardens the c (frankay for français), or adds one before e or i where it can never appear.

recorded.desc: The reception break beat. Same voice, same speed, back to back: [zhuh a-BEET] as an English reader says it with an audible gap, then j'habite as one unbroken word. The gap in take one must be long enough to hear without being a comic pause, around 250ms.

All fifteen contractions in list order: j'ai, m'appelle, t'aime, s'habiller, l'ami, l'école, d'accord, n'ai, qu'il, c'est, s'il, jusqu'à, lorsqu'il, puisqu'il, quelqu'un. Isolated, 900ms gaps, each one a single unbroken unit with no internal pause. This is the reference for what a contraction should sound like, so it must be flawless on that one point.

The trigger contrast: j'aime / je parle, j'arrive / le pain, l'eau / la porte, l'argent / de Paris, j'habite / je ne sais pas. CRITICAL: each pair must be one voice at one speed, recorded in a single take with a 400ms gap, because the whole teaching point is the presence or absence of the little uh of je. Two takes at different speeds makes the pair uncomparable and the section teaches nothing.

The h muet against h aspiré contrast, and the most important recording in the lesson: l'homme / le hibou, l'hôtel / le haricot, l'heure / la honte, l'hôpital / le hockey, plus l'ami / l'amie as an identical-sounding pair. CRITICAL: every pair must be the SAME voice at the SAME speed in ONE take, because the only difference is a gap of roughly 120ms and a listener cannot judge that across two takes. The aspiré side needs a real, audible, deliberate gap rather than a glottal stop.

All 10 example phrases, normal and 0.65 speed. At the slow speed the contractions must STAY contracted: slowing down is not permission to reintroduce the gap, and a slow take with a pause inside a contraction teaches the exact error the lesson removes.
All 12 dictation items, normal speed only, natural connected delivery. No exaggerated separation: the learner is being asked to hear a contraction as one word and write it as two-plus-apostrophe.

The 6-sentence reading passage, one take at natural pace, plus per-sentence stems for tap-to-replay. The two haricot instances must carry their blocked gap audibly, since one of the comprehension questions turns on it.

lessons.intro: French refuses to let two vowel sounds crash into each other. When a small word ending in a vowel meets a word starting with one, the first vowel is deleted and an apostrophe marks the place it stood. That is why it is j'aime and not je aime. This lesson gives you the fifteen words it happens to, the one thing that triggers it, and the short list of stubborn words that block it completely.

ipa.body: Sounds appear two ways in this course. IPA sits between slashes and is exact, the same alphabet linguists use worldwide: /ʒɛm/. The respelling sits between brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [ZHEM]. When the two disagree, trust the IPA. A small raised n, as in [PEHⁿ], marks a nasal vowel: the vowel goes through the nose, and it does NOT mean you should say an N. In this lesson a contracted form is respelled as one unbroken word, because that is exactly the claim being made about it.
ipa.title: The two notations, and what each is for

hMuet.body: Muet means mute. No H is pronounced anywhere in French, so this is not about sound: it is about whether the H BLOCKS things. An H muet does not block. The word behaves exactly as if the H were not written at all, so the vowel after it is the first sound and elision happens normally. le + homme gives l'homme, precisely as le + arbre gives l'arbre. Most French words beginning with H are muet, so this is the default and the safer guess when you genuinely do not know.
hMuet.title: H muet: the H that lets the word elide

examples.note: l'homme
l'hôtel
l'hôpital

elision.body: French does not like two vowel sounds meeting head on. When a small word ending in a vowel runs into a word starting with a vowel sound, the first vowel is deleted and an apostrophe marks the place it used to be. je + aime cannot stand, so the E goes and you get j'aime. That is elision. It is not an abbreviation and it is not optional or informal: writing je aime is simply an error, and saying it marks you out instantly. The apostrophe is not shorthand for a missing letter you might put back. It is a scar showing where a collision was avoided.
elision.title: Elision: the vowel that gets out of the way

examples.note: je + aime
la + école
ce + est

hAspire.body: Aspiré means breathed, and the name lies: an H aspiré is not breathed and makes no sound at all, exactly like an H muet. The only difference is that it BLOCKS. The word in front of it keeps its vowel, so you get le haricot and not l'haricot, la honte and not l'honte. Out loud this leaves a tiny gap where the elision would have been, and that gap is the only clue there is. Nothing in the spelling tells you which kind of H you are looking at. You learn each one with its article, the same way you learn a noun with its gender. The good news is that the aspiré list is short and mostly borrowed words.
hAspire.title: H aspiré: the H that blocks elision

examples.note: le haricot, blocked
le hibou, blocked
la honte, blocked

liaison.body: Elision deletes a vowel to stop two vowels colliding. Liaison does the opposite job for the opposite problem: it wakes a silent final consonant to fill a gap between two words. deux euros is said /dø.zø.ʁo/, with the X of deux coming back as a Z. Both exist for the same reason, which is that French wants a smooth, unbroken run of syllables and will move sounds around to get one. Elision removes something, liaison adds something, and the goal is identical. Liaison is your next lesson.
liaison.title: Liaison: the same instinct, solved the other way

examples.note: the article is welded on: no gap to fill

elidable.body: Elision is not a rule about all French words. It applies to a short, closed list of very small ones, and once you know the list you know every place it can happen: je, me, te, se, le, la, de, ne, que, ce. Add si, which elides only before il and ils, and the que compounds that inherit it: jusque, lorsque, puisque, quoique, quelque. That is the whole set. It never grows. Every other word in French keeps its vowel no matter what follows it, which is why la amie is wrong but ma amie is not (it is mon amie, for a different reason). Learn these fifteen and you have learned elision completely.
elidable.title: The closed list: which words actually do this

examples.note: je
de
si, only before il

apostrophe.body: In English an apostrophe usually marks a casual contraction you could undo: do not becomes don't, and both are fine. The French apostrophe is not that. It marks a deletion that is compulsory, and there is no version of the sentence where you put the letter back. j'ai has no formal alternative reading as je ai, because je ai is not French. Treat the apostrophe as glue rather than as a gap: the two words have become one unit with one stress and no pause anywhere inside it. Saying j'ai with a break in the middle is the single most common way to sound like you are reading rather than speaking.
apostrophe.title: What the apostrophe is actually doing

examples.note: one unit, no pause
two elisions, still no pause

vowelSound.body: This is the part that catches everyone. Elision is triggered by how the next word BEGINS OUT LOUD, not by how it is spelled. habite is spelled with an H, but the H is silent, so the word actually starts on the A sound: j'habite. The eye sees a consonant and the ear hears a vowel, and the ear is what decides. This is why you cannot work elision out from the page alone on any word starting with H. Every other letter in French tells you the truth: if the first letter is a vowel, the first sound is a vowel.
vowelSound.title: The trigger is a sound, not a letter

examples.note: H silent, so a vowel sound starts the word
same: the word starts on the O sound
a real consonant, so nothing drops

questions.q: l'ami and l'amie were both played. What told you which was which?
questions.why: Nothing. Both are /la.mi/. The elision deletes the article that carried the gender, so only spelling distinguishes them.

say.text: You know the rule now. What is left is the hesitation, and that is physical rather than intellectual.

sections.intro: Your eye sees two words and your mouth prepares two words. The apostrophe does not look like glue, so the reflex is to pause at it. That pause is what marks someone out as reading rather than speaking, and it is trained out by doing, not by knowing.
sections.title: Closing the gap

closing.text: A contraction is one word with one stress. When that is automatic, this lesson is done.

targets.label: The one-breath rule
steps: Look at the whole contraction and cover the apostrophe with a finger.
Say what is left as if it were one ordinary word.
Uncover it and say it again exactly the same way.
If a gap crept back in, cover it again. The apostrophe is glue, not a gap.

targets.label: The run-on
steps: Say the phrase deliberately too fast, faster than you can hesitate.
Notice that the contractions survive and only the pauses die.
Slow back down to normal speed while keeping every join closed.
Repeat until the slow version has no more gaps than the fast one.

targets.sub: For h aspiré, where a gap is correct
targets.label: The blocked gap
steps: Say le homme deliberately, with a gap. Hear how wrong it sounds.
Now say le hibou with exactly that same gap. It is correct.
Alternate the two until the gap feels like a decision rather than an accident.
The gap is not hesitation. It is the only thing marking an h aspiré.

say.text: Eight of them, scored on your voice. Conversation speed, and no gap anywhere.
Every line you say here has a contraction in it. Read your part out loud before you tap.

sections.title: Ordering, for real

turns.ai: Bonjour. Vous avez choisi ?
turns.en: Hello. Have you chosen?
turns.userEn: Yes, I have chosen.

alts.fr: Oui, je prends le menu du jour.

Yes, I have made my choice.

turns.ai: Très bien. Et comme boisson ?

sections.setting: A small restaurant in Lyon, one table free, the waiter already at your elbow.

say.text: Seven ways this goes wrong. You have probably made two of them this week.

errors.why: The commonest of all. Two vowels cannot meet, so the E of je is deleted. There is no version of French where the uncontracted form is acceptable.
errors.right: j'aime
errors.wrong: je aime

errors.why: h aspiré blocks the elision. The H is silent either way, but this one refuses to let the article contract.
errors.right: le haricot
errors.wrong: l'haricot

errors.why: h muet does not block. The word starts on the O sound, so the article contracts exactly as it would before any vowel.
errors.right: l'homme
errors.wrong: le homme

errors.why: tu is not on the closed list. You will hear t'as constantly in speech, but it is never correct in writing.
errors.right: tu as un stylo
errors.wrong: t'as un stylo (written)

errors.why: ma never elides. French solves that collision a different way, by switching to the masculine form mon before a vowel.
errors.right: mon amie
errors.wrong: m'amie

errors.why: One syllable, not two. Putting the uh back is what makes a fluent reader still sound like a beginner.
errors.right: j'ai [ZHAY]
errors.wrong: [zhuh-AY] for j'ai

errors.why: ne elides too, and this one carries the meaning. Say it uncontracted and a listener can genuinely miss the negative.
errors.right: je n'aime pas
errors.wrong: je ne aime pas

say.text: Read it out loud, all the way through, before you look at the questions.

sections.text: Aujourd'hui, j'arrive à l'hôtel à neuf heures. L'homme à la réception me demande mon nom. Je m'appelle Marie, et j'habite à Lyon depuis un an. Il n'y a pas d'ascenseur, alors je monte l'escalier jusqu'à la chambre. C'est une petite chambre, mais l'eau est chaude et la fenêtre donne sur le parc. Le soir, je descends. Le restaurant sert du poulet et des haricots verts. Je n'aime pas beaucoup les haricots, mais j'ai faim, alors je demande l'addition sans rien dire.
sections.title: A paragraph of it

glossary.note: le + ascenseur. Contracted, like every vowel-initial noun.
le + escalier.
jusque + à. A que compound, so it behaves like que.
h aspiré, so no liaison and no elision. A tiny gap after les.

questions.a: Aujourd'hui (a frozen one, from de), j'arrive (je + arrive) and l'hôtel (le + hôtel). Three in eight words.
questions.q: Find every elision in the first sentence and say what each one contracted from.

questions.a: haricot is h aspiré. It blocks the elision AND the liaison, so the S of les stays silent and you leave a small gap.
questions.q: Why is it « les haricots » with a gap, and not « les-z-haricots »?

questions.a: None in sound: neither H is pronounced. The difference is purely grammatical. homme is h muet so the article contracts; haricot is h aspiré so it does not.
questions.q: The passage has « l'homme » and « les haricots ». Both start with H. What is the difference?

questions.a: There is no such sentence here: both negatives (n'y a pas, n'aime pas) sit before a vowel and both contract. If the next word had started on a consonant, ne would have stayed whole.
questions.q: Find the sentence where « ne » does NOT contract, and explain why.

questions.a: None inside the contractions. j'ai and l'addition are each one unbroken unit, and the only natural break is at the comma.
questions.q: Read the last sentence aloud. How many separate pauses should there be inside it?

Fifteen: je me te se le la de ne que ce, plus si and four que compounds.
A vowel SOUND on the next word. Not a vowel letter.
The H is silent, so habite begins on a vowel sound. The ear decides, not the eye.
cards.front: Why it is j'habite and not je habite

cards.back: Blocks the elision. le haricot, le hibou, la honte, never l'.
You cannot. Learn each aspiré word with its article.

cards.back: Muet. It is far more common, and most aspiré words are recent borrowings.

cards.back: Glue, not a gap. One word, one stress, no pause inside it.
No. Both /la.mi/. Elision hides the gender completely.

sections.body: An hour ago the apostrophe was punctuation you copied. Now it is a rule you can apply to a word you have never seen, in both directions: you know when it must appear and when it must not. The H list is the only part that is memory rather than logic, and it is eight words long. Everything else in this lesson is one question asked quickly.

stats.v: Liaison, the same instinct in reverse

sections.title: Where you are

say.text: Round one. The basic move, in both directions.

questions.q: Which of these is correct French?
questions.why: je + aime collide, so the E of je is deleted and the apostrophe marks the spot. je aime is not a form French has.

questions.q: Type the contracted form of « je » + « ai ».
questions.why: The E of je is deleted before the vowel of ai. Two letters and an apostrophe, said as one syllable.

questions.q: Why does « je parle » keep its E?
questions.why: Elision only happens when two vowel SOUNDS would collide. The P of parle is a consonant, so there is no collision and nothing gives way.

questions.q: Say the contracted form: I live.
questions.why: One unbroken word, no gap after the J sound. A pause in the middle is the thing this lesson exists to remove.

questions.q: A learner writes « le ami ». Fix it.
questions.why: le + ami is a vowel collision, so the E of le drops. The article and the noun become one unit.

questions.q: Which word did you hear?
questions.why: j'aime is one syllable with no gap. je parle has two, with the little uh of je clearly audible.

questions.q: Type what « la » + « école » becomes.
questions.why: The A of la is deleted before the vowel of école. Note that the feminine gender becomes invisible: nothing on the page still says la.

questions.q: How many syllables in « c'est » ?
questions.why: One. /sɛ/. ce + est contracted to a single syllable, which is why it is the most common word in spoken French.

say.text: Round two. Which words do this, and which only look like they should.

questions.q: Which of these words NEVER elides?
questions.why: tu is not on the list. It keeps its vowel always: tu as, never t'as in writing. de, ne and que all elide.

questions.q: Type the contracted form of « ne » + « ai » in « je ... pas ».
questions.why: ne is on the list, so it elides before a vowel: je n'ai pas. Drop the elision and the negative disappears with it.
questions.answer: n'ai, as in je n'ai pas

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
questions.why: Two collisions, two elisions. ne + ai and de + argent both contract, and neither one is optional.
opts: Je ne ai pas de argent.

questions.q: Say it: my name is Marie.
questions.why: me + appelle contracts to m'appelle. The first sentence you ever learned in French was an elision.

questions.q: What does « s'il vous plaît » contract from?
questions.why: si + il. And si is a special case: it elides before il and ils, and nowhere else in the language.

questions.q: A learner writes « que est-ce que ce est ». Fix the two elisions.
questions.why: que + est and ce + est both collide. The second que survives untouched because a consonant follows it.

questions.q: Type the contracted form of « de » + « accord ».
questions.why: You have been saying this since your first week without noticing it was two words.

questions.q: Which is right: « le hamster » or « l'hamster »?
questions.why: hamster is a borrowed word, and borrowed words almost always take h aspiré. The article stays whole.

say.text: Round three. The hard part. Nothing on the page will help you here.

questions.q: Which one blocks the elision?
questions.why: hibou is h aspiré, so the article stays whole. The other three are h muet and elide normally.

questions.q: Say it: the bean.
questions.why: le haricot, with a small gap between le and aricot. Closing that gap turns it into a word French does not have.

questions.q: Which word did you hear?
questions.why: The gap before the vowel is the only difference, and it is the only signal there is.

questions.q: A learner writes « l'haricot ». Fix it.
questions.why: h aspiré blocks the elision. The article keeps its vowel even though the H is completely silent.

questions.q: How do you tell an h muet from an h aspiré by looking at the word?
questions.why: Nothing in the spelling distinguishes them and neither is pronounced. You learn each aspiré word with its article, the way you learn a noun with its gender.
opts: you cannot, you learn each one

questions.q: Type the correct article plus noun: « honte » (shame).
questions.why: honte is h aspiré, so la keeps its vowel. It is one of the eight worth memorising outright.

questions.q: Which is correct?
questions.why: hôpital is h muet, so the article elides. Compare le hockey, which is aspiré and does not.

questions.q: Say it: the man does not like the bean.
questions.why: Both H words in one sentence: l'homme elides, le haricot blocks. Getting both right in one breath is the whole skill.

say.text: Round four. Elision is invisible in one word and obvious in a phrase.

questions.q: Type the sentence: The bill, please.
questions.why: Two elisions in five words, and you have been saying both correctly for weeks.

questions.q: Say it: it is time.
questions.why: C'est l'heure. Two contractions and no pause anywhere in it.

questions.q: How many elisions are in « Je n'ai pas d'argent »?
questions.why: ne + ai and de + argent. je keeps its E because n is a consonant.

questions.q: A learner says « Je ne aime pas ». Fix it.
questions.why: ne + aime collide, so ne elides. Leaving it whole is the mistake that most often makes a negative sound like a positive.

questions.q: Which sentence has NO elision in it at all?
questions.why: Je ne sais pas: sais starts on a consonant, so ne keeps its vowel. Nothing in it collides.

questions.q: Type what you hear.
questions.why: A frozen elision. Nobody has said hui as a separate word in five hundred years, but the apostrophe still marks the join.

questions.q: Say it: today, I arrive at the hotel.
questions.why: Three contractions running: aujourd'hui, j'arrive, l'hôtel. None of them takes a pause.

questions.q: Which is correct?
questions.why: de + eau collide, so de elides. This is the free water you can ask for in any French restaurant.

say.text: Last round. This one is about speed, not knowledge.

questions.q: What is the apostrophe in « j'ai » actually marking?
questions.why: A deleted vowel, and the deletion is compulsory. Unlike an English contraction there is no fuller form you could use instead.

questions.q: Say it: what is that?
questions.why: Four written words, three syllables, no pause. If you can say this at speed you have the rule.

questions.q: Type the contracted form of « me » + « appelle ».
questions.why: me is on the closed list and behaves exactly like je, te and se.

questions.q: Which pair sounds IDENTICAL out loud?
questions.why: Both are /la.mi/. The elision hides the gender completely, so only the spelling tells you which friend it is.

questions.q: A learner says [zhuh-AY] for « j'ai ». Fix the delivery.
questions.why: The contraction is one syllable. Putting the uh of je back is the single most common way to sound like you are reading aloud.

questions.q: Why do elision and liaison exist?
questions.why: Both stop a French phrase from stumbling between two words. Elision deletes a vowel, liaison wakes a consonant, and the goal is the same.
opts: to keep speech smooth between vowels

questions.q: Type what you hear.
questions.why: ne + est contracts. ce keeps its vowel because an N follows it, not a vowel.

questions.q: Say it: I have no money.
questions.why: Two elisions and a negative. Say it at conversation speed or it does not count.

say.text: That is the lesson. Four things worth keeping, and the last one is where you go next.

sections.body: An hour ago you said two words where French says one, and a receptionist waited for you to finish a sentence you thought you had finished. The fix was not vocabulary. It was one rule about what French does when two vowels meet, a list of fifteen small words it applies to, and eight stubborn H words that refuse. You now do this without deciding to, which is the only version of it that is any use in a conversation.
sections.title: What you take with you
points: Two vowels collide, the little word gives way. That is elision, and it is compulsory rather than casual.
Fifteen words do it: je me te se le la de ne que ce, plus si and the que compounds. Nothing else in French elides.
The trigger is a vowel SOUND, not a vowel letter. That is why it is j'habite, and why you cannot read elision off the page for any H word.
Eight H words block it outright: le haricot, le hibou, la honte and the rest. Guess muet when you do not know, and learn the aspiré ones with their article.
Next lesson is the same instinct running the other way. When a gap opens between two words, French wakes a sleeping consonant to fill it. That is liaison.

segments.text: I am Camille. Today we are doing elision, which is the reason French words run into each other the way they do.
You already do this correctly several times a day without knowing it. By the end you will do it on purpose.
C'est parti.
One idea first. French does not let two vowel sounds meet head on. When they would, the small word in front loses its vowel.
je aime
That is not French. The two vowels collide, so the E of je is deleted and you get this instead.
j'aime
Fifteen small words do this. Here are the four you will use most.
j'ai
c'est
d'accord
l'école
Each one is a single syllable or a single unbroken unit. No pause where the apostrophe is.
Now the thing that decides it. Listen to these two and tell me which one contracted.
j'habite
je parle
The first one. habite starts with an H, but the H is silent, so out loud the word begins on a vowel. The ear decides, never the spelling.
Your turn. Say: I live in Lyon.
Again, and this time the bill, please.
One trap before we finish. A short list of H words block all of this. Which of these is correct?
le haricot
le haricot, with the article whole and a small gap after it. Never l'haricot, however wrong that looks.
Three things to keep. Two vowels collide, the little word gives way. Fifteen words do it and nothing else does.
And the trigger is a sound, not a letter, which is why eight stubborn H words can block the whole thing.
À bientôt.

errorTriggers.description: Writes or says the uncontracted form: je aime, le ami, de argent.
Elides a word that is not on the closed list, or fails to elide one that is.
Elides before an h aspiré (l'haricot) or blocks before an h muet (le homme).
Produces the contraction with an audible gap: [zhuh-AY] for j'ai.

les‿amis, vous‿avez, nous‿avons, ils‿ont, deux‿enfants, chez‿elle. Isolated, 900ms gaps. The Z must be audibly VOICED and audibly attached to the second word, not the first.
c'est‿un, quand‿il, petit‿ami, grand‿arbre, quand‿elle, tout‿à fait. Isolated, 900ms gaps. On grand and quand the release must be a clean T with no D colouring.
mon‿ami, un‿homme, en‿avion, un‿an, attends un‿instant, mon‿ami travaille. The nasal vowel must stay nasal UNDER the new N. A flattened vowel is the error being taught against.

CONTRAST SET, one voice one session. les‿amis correct then [less a-MEE] wrong; grand‿arbre with T then with D; deux‿enfants with Z then with KS; neuf‿heures with V then with F. Each pair adjacent, 400ms apart, both speeds.

CONTRAST SET, one voice one session. et il, et elle, en haut, un restaurant italien, un enfant intelligent, Jean arrive, les onze. Every one UNLINKED, with an audible gap. Then quand‿il linked, adjacent, so the learner hears et against quand.

CONTRAST SET, one voice one session, HIGHEST PRIORITY. les‿amis linked against les héros unlinked; un‿homme linked against un hasard unlinked; les‿hommes against les haricots. Members of each pair adjacent, 400ms gap, both speeds. Device TTS links héros, so until this lands the card teaches the opposite of the rule.

CONTRAST SET, one voice one session. ils‿ont / ils sont, vous‿avez / vous savez, un‿an / cent ans, quand‿il / et il, les‿Anglais / Jean arrive, très‿intéressant / toujours intéressant. Adjacent, 400ms, both speeds. These are only teaching objects if the two members are audibly different.

REGISTER SET, one voice one session, both members mandatory. Je suis allé unlinked (courant) then linked (soutenu); Nous sommes arrivés unlinked then linked; Il faut aller unlinked then linked. The pair carries the whole teaching point, so a take with only one member is unusable.
The 12 dictation items, normal speed only, natural connected delivery. The liaison must be produced as it would be in running speech, not as two carefully separated words.
The 5-line weekend message, normal and slow, plus per-line stems. Natural pace: the joins are the difficulty and slowing the delivery removes the exercise.
The 6-sentence reading passage, one take, plus per-sentence stems for tap-to-replay. Fourteen liaisons and two blocked joins, all at natural speed.

lessons.intro: French does not leave its words where the spaces are. A consonant that is silent at the end of one word wakes up when the next word starts with a vowel, and it lands on the front of that next word rather than staying where it was written. That single habit is why fluent French sounds like one continuous stream, and learning it changes your listening more than any other hour in this track. This lesson gives you the three consonants that do it, what each one turns into on the way across, and the short list of joins French keeps sealed.

ipa.body: IPA sits in slashes and is exact: /le.z‿a.mi/. The respelling sits in brackets and is a reading aid for an English speaker, with the stressed syllable capitalised: [lay-z‿a-MEE]. When the two disagree, the IPA is right. A nasal vowel is written with a superscript n, as in [ahⁿ], because it is one sound made through the nose and not a vowel followed by an N. The tie ‿ appears in both notations and always means the same thing: a liaison lands here.
ipa.title: How to read the sounds in this course

examples.note: both notations, same word

tie.body: The little curve in les‿amis is a tie, and it marks a liaison. It sits between the two words in the spelling and between the two sounds in the IPA. Read it as "this consonant belongs to the word on the left but is pronounced at the start of the word on the right". That second half is the part learners miss: the Z of les does not end les, it begins amis. Say lay-ZAMEE, not LAYZ amee. The tie is telling you where to put the sound, not just that a sound exists.
tie.title: The tie mark: where the sound actually lands

examples.note: the Z starts amis, it does not end les
deux enfants, same shape

hAspire.body: French never pronounces an H. Not in any word, not in any position. But some words behave as though an invisible wall sits at the front of them, and those are the h aspiré words: they block liaison and they block elision. les héros keeps its silent S and stays two separate sounds, while les hommes links straight through. Nothing in the spelling distinguishes them, and there is no rule to derive: you learn which H a word has at the same time you learn the word, exactly the way you learn a noun with its gender. The good news is the list is short and the common ones repeat.
hAspire.title: H aspiré: the H that blocks the link

examples.note: les héros, blocked
un homme, h muet, links
en haut, blocked

liaison.body: A liaison is a final consonant that is silent when the word stands alone and comes back when the next word starts with a vowel. les on its own is /le/, with no S. les amis is /le.z‿a.mi/, and the S is suddenly there, as a Z, attached to the front of amis. Nothing about the spelling changes. The letter was always written; the vowel next door is what wakes it. This is the same silent consonant you spent the last lesson learning to leave out, which is why liaison feels like a contradiction until you see that the rule was never silent always, it was silent unless something wakes it.
liaison.title: Liaison: the consonant that wakes up

examples.note: les amis, the S returns as a Z
c'est un, the T returns
mon ami, the N returns

devoicing.body: A woken consonant does not always return as the letter that was written. S and X both come back as /z/, which is why les amis is lay-Z-amee and not lay-S-amee, and why deux enfants has a Z in it. D comes back as /t/, so grand arbre is grahⁿ-T-arbr with no D sound anywhere. F comes back as /v/ in neuf heures. Only T, N and L return as themselves. So the spelling tells you THAT something wakes up; it does not reliably tell you WHAT wakes up, and that mismatch is where half the errors in this lesson live.
devoicing.title: The letter is not the sound it comes back as

examples.note: S returns as Z
D returns as T
X returns as Z

interdite.body: Some gaps are sealed, and linking across them is an error rather than a flourish. The list is short enough to learn: et never links, ever, in any register. A word beginning with an h aspiré blocks the link even though the H makes no sound. A singular noun does not link to the adjective after it. A personal name does not link to its verb. The numbers onze and un-as-a-number behave like h aspiré words. This is the half of liaison that over-eager learners get wrong, because once you have learned to link, linking everything feels like progress.
interdite.title: Interdite: you must NOT link

examples.note: et il, never linked
les héros, blocked by h aspiré
singular noun, then adjective

facultative.body: A third group is genuinely optional. Both versions are correct French, and the choice signals how formal you are being: a broadcaster or a politician links them, two friends in a kitchen do not. Je suis allé can be said with the link or without it and nobody is wrong. At your level the useful thing is to know the category exists so it does not confuse you when you hear the same sentence two ways. Your safe default is to leave optional liaisons alone. Skipping one sounds relaxed and native. Adding a forbidden one sounds like a mistake, so the risk is not symmetric.
facultative.title: Facultative: optional, and about register

examples.note: the everyday version, no link
the formal version, linked

obligatoire.body: Some liaisons are compulsory. Leaving one out does not sound casual, it sounds wrong, and in a few cases it changes the word. These are the ones worth drilling to reflex. The pattern behind almost all of them is that the two words belong to one grammatical unit: an article and its noun, a subject pronoun and its verb, a possessive and its noun, an adjective sitting in front of its noun, or a fixed expression that French treats as a single block. If the two words are glued together by grammar, they are glued together in sound.
obligatoire.title: Obligatoire: you must link

examples.note: article and noun
pronoun and verb
adjective in front of its noun

sections.body: Every gap between two French words has one of three answers: you must link, you must not, or it is up to you. Almost every gap you meet is the first. The second is a short list worth memorising. The third is about how formal you are being, and you can safely ignore it while you are learning.
sections.title: Three answers, not two

sections.body: Optional liaisons are correct either way and signal formality. Je suis allé, nous sommes arrivés, il faut aller. Leave them unlinked while you are learning. Skipping an optional liaison sounds relaxed and native; adding a forbidden one sounds like an error, so when you are unsure the cheap mistake and the expensive mistake are not the same size.

sections.body: A liaison consonant sits between two vowels once it moves across, and a consonant between two vowels is easier to say voiced than unvoiced. That is the whole reason /s/ becomes /z/ and /f/ becomes /v/. You do not need the phonetics to use it, but it explains why the change is consistent rather than arbitrary: French did not pick these at random, the mouth did.
sections.title: Why the S softens

sections.body: The mark in les‿amis is a tie. It appears in both the IPA and the respelling, and it always means the same thing: a liaison lands here. Read it as an instruction about placement. The consonant before the tie is written as part of the first word and pronounced as part of the second. If your screen shows a box or a blank instead of a small curve, tell us: the mark is doing real work and a missing glyph erases it.
sections.title: Reading the tie

overview.introFr: En français, une consonne finale muette se réveille quand le mot suivant commence par une voyelle, et elle se prononce au début de ce mot. Dans cette leçon, vous apprenez les trois consonnes de liaison, ce qu'elles deviennent, et les cas où la liaison est interdite.
overview.titleEn: Liaison: the consonant that moves to the next word

say.text: You spent a whole lesson learning that French does not say its final consonants. This morning one of them came back, and it took a sentence with it.

say.text: Six things. Every one of them is something you do out loud, not something you can only recognise.

goals.s: Say les amis, vous avez, deux enfants and nous avons with the S and X coming back as a Z on the front of the next word.
Say c'est un, quand il and tout à fait without hesitating at the join.
Say mon ami and un homme with the N appearing and the nasal vowel still intact underneath it.
Know that S and X wake as Z and D wakes as T, so les amis never comes out as less amis.
Say et il, les héros and un enfant intelligent with the gap left open, because French forbids the link.
Catch vous avez as three words rather than one noise, at full speed, in a sentence you have not seen.

cards.body: That is the whole lesson. Last lesson gave you the default: silent. This lesson gives you the one thing that overrides it, and it is not a property of the word, it is the word that comes next.
cards.head: The letter was never gone. It was waiting for a vowel.

cards.body: The consonant only wakes if the next word starts with a vowel sound. Consonant next door, and it stays asleep: les tickets keeps its S silent, les amis does not.
cards.head: A vowel is the alarm clock

cards.body: This is the part that fixes your ear. In les‿amis the Z does not end les, it starts amis. You are saying lay-ZAMEE. That is why French sounds like one long word: the joins are in the wrong places.
cards.head: The sound moves forward

cards.body: S and X wake up as a Z. D wakes up as a T. F wakes up as a V. Only T, N and L come back as themselves, so the spelling tells you that something happens, not what.
cards.head: The letter changes on the way up

cards.body: Some links are compulsory, some are forbidden, and some are optional. The forbidden ones are a short list and they are where the errors are.

sections.body: A final consonant wakes when the next word begins with a vowel, and it lands on the front of that word. The letter was never gone. It was waiting for a vowel. Nothing about the first word changed. What changed is next door.

say.text: You have spent half an hour learning to link. Now the other half of the rule, and it is the half that trips people. In each of these the consonant is right there and French refuses to use it.

cards.tip: The one to learn first. et has a silent T and it stays silent in every register, forever.

say.text: Not linking is harder than linking, because by now the link is the reflex you just built. What you are training here is the override, and it is physical.

sections.intro: For the last half hour you have been rewarded every time you joined two words. That reflex is now running faster than your judgement, which is exactly what you wanted, and exactly what makes the forbidden set hard. You cannot fix this by knowing the rule. You fix it by practising the stop until the stop is also a reflex.
sections.title: Training the stop

closing.text: The letter was never gone. It was waiting for a vowel. And in these cases the vowel arrives and the letter still does not come, because French has decided this particular join is closed. Practise the stop for thirty seconds a day and it stops being a decision.

targets.sub: For every et before a vowel
targets.label: The et stop
steps: Read the phrase to yourself and find the et.
Say the word before et, then stop completely. Close your mouth.
Start et as though it were the first word of a new sentence.
Run the two halves together at speed, keeping the gap.
Repeat until leaving the gap costs you no effort at all.

targets.sub: For any word starting with H
targets.label: The h aspiré pair test
steps: Say the word with les in front of it, linked, as though it were h muet.
Say it again with the gap left open.
Pick the one you have actually heard from a French speaker.
If you have never heard it, treat it as h muet and link: that is the more common kind.
Bank the exceptions as a list. There are fewer than twenty you will meet this year.

targets.sub: For a singular noun followed by an adjective
targets.label: The noun-adjective stop
steps: Find the noun and the adjective after it.
Ask whether the adjective is BEFORE or AFTER the noun.
Before the noun, link it. After the noun, leave it.
Say the phrase both ways and notice how wrong the linked version sounds once you know.

say.text: Every one of these is a good instinct pointed slightly wrong. Most of them come from applying something you learned correctly, one step too far.

errors.why: You linked, which was right, and you used the letter that was written, which felt right. French softens that S all the way to a Z. The mechanical step was correct and the sound was not.
errors.right: les amis /le.z‿a.mi/ [lay-z‿a-MEE]
errors.wrong: les amis said as [less a-MEE]

errors.why: You put the Z at the end of les instead of the start of amis. English joins words at their edges; French moves the consonant forward into the next word, and that is why French sounds like one continuous stream to you.
errors.right: les amis [lay-z‿a-MEE]
errors.wrong: les amis said as [LAYZ a-MEE]

errors.why: The word is spelled with a D so you said a D. A final D always wakes up as a T. There is no French word where a linking D stays a D.
errors.right: grand arbre [grahⁿ-t‿ARBR]
errors.wrong: grand arbre said as [grahⁿ-D-ARBR]

errors.why: By this point in the lesson linking is your reflex, and et has a T sitting right there. It is the one word in French that never links, and the reflex you just built is exactly what makes this error.
errors.right: et il [AY EEL]
errors.wrong: et il said as [ay-T-EEL]

errors.why: You applied the les rule faithfully. héros carries an h aspiré, which blocks the link, and nothing in the spelling tells you that. This is learned word by word, not derived.
errors.right: les héros [LAY ay-ROH]
errors.wrong: les héros said as [lay-Z-ay-ROH]

errors.why: The first link is compulsory and the second is forbidden. A singular noun does not link to the adjective after it, so the same sentence needs two opposite decisions two words apart.
errors.right: un enfant intelligent [uhⁿ-n‿ahⁿ-FAHⁿ ehⁿ-tay-lee-ZHAHⁿ]
errors.wrong: un enfant intelligent linked twice

errors.why: You added the N and flattened the nasal vowel to get there. The nasal stays: you are adding a consonant, not trading the vowel for one.
errors.right: mon ami [mohⁿ-n‿a-MEE]
errors.wrong: mon ami said as [moh-na-MEE]

errors.why: Once linking feels like progress, more of it feels like more progress. Over-linking is the most common marker of a learner who has just studied this topic, and the safe default is the opposite of the instinct.
errors.right: leaving optional liaisons alone
errors.wrong: linking every optional liaison

say.text: Before the quiz, look at what changed in the last hour.

sections.body: An hour ago a French sentence was one continuous noise and you could not find the word boundaries in it. The reason was not speed. It was that French moves consonants across the gaps, so the joins you were listening for are not where the spaces are. You now know which consonants move, what they turn into on the way, and which gaps stay shut. That is the single biggest step available in French listening, and it is why this lesson sits where it does.
