questions.q: Of everything this track has taught, which rule applies last, after all the others?
questions.a: Rhythm. The other rules decide which sounds are there; rhythm decides how they are spaced once they are. That is why it is the last lesson before the Masterclass: it sits on top of everything else.

questions.q: Read the last sentence aloud. How many pushes did you make?
questions.a: One per group. Count the rows in the respelling: each | is a break, and each group ends on the CAPS syllable.

say.text: Not the sentences, the system. If you keep four things, keep these.

cards.front: What is the rule, in one line?
cards.back: Even syllables, then one push at the end.

cards.front: Where does the push go in a long sentence?
cards.back: At the end of each GROUP, not once at the end of the sentence. A three-group sentence has three pushes.

cards.front: What does English do that French does not?
cards.back: Stretch the important syllable and collapse the rest to uh. French keeps every syllable at full value, which is why it can sound fast.

cards.front: How do you turn a statement into a question?
cards.back: Take the final syllable upward instead of downward. No word changes.
Yes. "On mange, les enfants" and "On mange les enfants" are the same five syllables and are not the same sentence.

say.text: Six things that go wrong, in the order you are likely to hit them.

errors.wrong: JE voudrais un CA-fé
errors.right: je vou-drais un ca-FÉ
errors.why: The English instinct: push the words that carry meaning. French pushes by position, always at the end of the group.

errors.wrong: Swallowing the middle: "s'il vous plaît" as "svouplé"
errors.right: seel voo PLEH, all three syllables at full value
errors.why: English reduces unstressed syllables to uh and drops them. French does not reduce, so the syllables you would swallow in English have to stay.

errors.wrong: One push at the very end of a long sentence
errors.right: One push at the end of every group
errors.why: This is the most common half-learned version of the rule. It makes a long sentence sound like one enormous word.

errors.wrong: A dramatic pause at the comma
errors.right: A short breath, about two tenths of a second
errors.why: The break is a boundary, not a silence. Too long and the sentence sounds like two sentences.

errors.wrong: Ending a question flat
errors.right: Taking the last syllable upward
errors.why: In French the contour can be the only thing marking a question. Flat means statement, and it gets answered as one.

errors.wrong: Speeding up in the middle of a long phrase
errors.right: The same syllable length from the first to the last
errors.why: Rushing the middle is English rhythm reappearing under pressure. Even means even the whole way, including the boring parts.

sections.title: Where you are

say.text: Before the quiz, a quick look at what you have covered.

sections.body: Five acts done. You have gone from three-syllable phrases to fifteen, and from one group to three. The quiz is mostly listening and speaking, because that is the only way to test something you cannot see.

stats.v: Short phrases, said flat, with nothing swallowed
At the end of the group, not on the important word
Heard by ear, and it can change the meaning
Up for a question, down for a statement

say.text: Five rounds. Most of them ask you to listen or to speak, because rhythm is not something you can prove on paper.
Eight on the basic shape. Two of them ask you to speak, so find somewhere you can talk out loud.

questions.q: What does French do to the syllables in a phrase?
opts: Gives every one the same length
Stretches the important ones, shortens the rest
questions.why: Every syllable keeps its full value. That is why nothing gets reduced to uh the way it does in English, and it is why French can sound fast without anything being skipped.

questions.q: Listen. How many syllables did you hear?
questions.why: Three, and all three the same length. Counting them is the first skill: an English ear tends to hear the stretched one as "the" syllable and lose the others.

questions.q: Say it: "Il fait froid."
questions.why: Three syllables, all the same length, and the last one held slightly longer. [eel feh FRWA]

questions.q: In English, what happens to an unstressed syllable?
questions.why: English reduces unstressed vowels to schwa: the second syllable of photograph is not the vowel it is spelled with. French does not reduce, so every syllable you would swallow in English has to survive.

questions.q: Listen. Which syllable was held the longest?
questions.why: The last, and only slightly. If you heard a middle syllable stand out, that was an English ear supplying a stress the speaker did not make.

questions.q: Say it: "Tu lis trop."
questions.why: Flat and even, then hold the last one. [tü lee TROH]

questions.q: Which of these is the rule, in one line?
opts: Even syllables, then one push at the end.
Stress the word that matters most
questions.why: Even syllables, then one push at the end. That is the whole system, and everything else in the lesson follows from it.

questions.q: Listen to the four-syllable phrase. How many syllables were held longer than the others?
questions.why: Exactly one, the last. If you heard two, one of them was an English stress arriving early.

say.text: Eight on placement. This is the round that catches the English instinct.

questions.q: Where does the push go in a French rhythm group?
opts: On the last syllable of the group
On the word that carries the meaning
questions.why: By position, never by meaning. French does not move the push to the important word, which is exactly what English does and why the English version is so recognisable.

questions.q:
This reading is WRONG: [EEL pluh boh-koo duh-ohr]

"Il pleut beaucoup dehors."

Type the word that should carry the push instead.
questions.why: The push goes on the last word of the group, not on the word that carries the meaning. [eel pluh boh-koo duh-OHR]

questions.q: Listen. Which word did the voice hold at the end?
questions.why: The last word of the group, every time. French marks the end by position and lets the words carry their own weight, where English would lean on whichever word it thought mattered.

questions.q: Say it, with the push at the end: "L'air froid pique fort dehors."
questions.why: Everything even, then hold the final syllable only. [lehr frwa peek fohr duh-OHR]

questions.q:
This reading is WRONG: [LUH grahⁿ lee eh kohⁿ-fohr-tabl]

"Le grand lit est confortable."

Type the word that should carry the push instead.
questions.why: The push landed early, on the first content word. That is the English instinct. It belongs on the group-final syllable: [luh grahⁿ lee eh kohⁿ-fohr-TABL]

questions.q: Does the push make the syllable louder?
opts: Yes, and the others get quieter
No, it is held slightly longer
questions.why: It is a lengthening, not a stress. Nothing gets louder and nothing else gets quieter, which is why it sounds so different from English emphasis.

questions.q: Listen. Where did the push land?
questions.why: At the end of the group, as always. Whatever the sentence is about, the position does not move.

questions.q: Say it: "Je bois un chocolat chaud."
questions.why: Resist the urge to lean on the word that matters. [zhuh bwa uhⁿ shoh-koh-la SHOH]

say.text: Eight on direction. Same words, different endings.

questions.q: How does French mark a question with no extra word and no inversion?
opts: By taking the final syllable upward
questions.why: The contour alone can carry it. That is why a flat question gets answered as a statement: nothing else in the sentence marked it.

questions.q: Listen. Was that a question or a statement?
questions.why: The final syllable went up. Everything before it was as flat as a statement, which is exactly the point: the direction is the only clue.

questions.q: Say it as a question: "Tu viens demain ?"
questions.why: Flat and even all the way, then up on the last syllable only. [tü vyaⁿ duh-MAⁿ]

questions.q: Listen. Was that a question or a statement?
questions.why: The final syllable fell. Same rhythm as the question, opposite direction on one syllable.

questions.q: What happens to the syllables BEFORE the final one in a question?
opts: They stay flat, exactly as in a statement
questions.why: The rise is on the last syllable only. Learners often ramp the whole phrase upward, which sounds like surprise rather than a question.

questions.q: Say it as a question: "Vous partez déjà ?"
questions.why: Do not ramp the whole phrase. Flat, flat, flat, then up. [voo par-tay day-ZHA]

questions.q: Listen. Does this want an answer, or agreement?
opts: An answer: it is a question
questions.why: It rose on the last syllable, so it is a question and it wants an answer. A falling ending would be a statement, wanting agreement, with not one word changed.

questions.q: Listen. The speaker meant it as a question. Did it land as one?
questions.why: A flat ending reads as a statement whatever the speaker intended. This is the single most common way a French question fails to be heard as one.

say.text: Eight on grouping. This is where the push stops being simple, and where it can change what you said.

questions.q: A sentence breaks into three groups. How many pushes does it get?
questions.why: One per group. The half-learned version of this rule puts a single push at the end of the sentence, which makes a long sentence sound like one enormous word.

questions.q: "On mange les enfants." said as ONE group. What does it mean?
questions.why: One group makes les enfants the object: they are the meal. Breaking after mange turns them into who you are speaking to. Five syllables either way, and the break is the only difference.

questions.q: Listen. How many groups did the voice break this into?
opts: Two, with a breath in the middle
questions.why: Two, breaking after mange. That break is what turns les enfants into who you are speaking TO rather than what you are eating. One group would mean the other thing.

questions.q:
"J'ai trop froid ce matin je reste sous les draps."

The voice breathes once. Type the LAST WORD before the break.
questions.why: You can hear it without seeing it: the voice holds that syllable, breathes, then starts flat again. [zhay troh frwa suh ma-TAⁿ | zhuh rehst soo lay DRA]

questions.q: Listen. How many groups?

audio.clip: Après le travail, il rentre, et il dort.

questions.why: Count the holds, not the words. Each lengthening followed by a short breath is the end of a group.

questions.q: Say it with all three pushes: "Le matin, je me lève, et je pars."
questions.target: Le matin, je me lève, et je pars.
questions.ipa: /lə ma.tɛ̃ | ʒə mə lɛv | e ʒə paʁ/
questions.why: Not three separate sentences: one sentence that breathes twice. [luh ma-TAⁿ | zhuh muh LEHV | ay zhuh PAR]

questions.q: How long is the break between groups?
opts: There is no gap at all
As long as the speaker likes
About two tenths of a second
questions.why: A boundary, not a silence. Stretch it and the sentence stops sounding like one sentence.

questions.q:
"Le soir je lis un peu."

Type the LAST WORD before the break.
questions.why: The break follows the sense: the first group sets the scene and the second says what happened. [luh SWAR | zhuh lee uhⁿ PUH]

say.text: The last eight. Long phrases, everything stacked, and mostly by ear.

questions.q: Listen to the twelve-syllable sentence. What went wrong in the middle?

audio.clip: Après le repas, on marche dans le parc.

questions.why: Rushing the middle is English rhythm reappearing under pressure. Even means even the whole way, including the parts that feel like filler.

questions.q:
This reading is WRONG: [EEL eh tar | luh puh-tee vee-lazh dohr soo la nehzh]

"Il est tard, le petit village dort sous la neige."

Type the word that should carry the push instead.
questions.why: The first group lost its push and the sentence ran on as if it were one group. [eel eh TAR | luh puh-tee vee-lazh dohr soo la NEHZH]

questions.q: Listen. Where does the voice breathe in this one?
opts: It does not, it runs straight through

audio.clip: Ce soir, il rentre très tard.

questions.why: Once. The other rules of this track decide which sounds exist; rhythm decides how they are spaced, and the breath is where the spacing shows.

questions.q: Say the whole thing: "Ce soir, on mange tôt, puis on sort."
questions.target: Ce soir, on mange tôt, puis on sort.
questions.ipa: /sə swaʁ | ɔ̃ mɑ̃ʒ to | pɥi ɔ̃ sɔʁ/
questions.why: Three groups, three pushes, no speeding up in the middle. [suh SWAR | ohⁿ mahⁿzh TOH | pwee ohⁿ SOHR]

questions.q:
This reading is WRONG: [TÜ par too-zhoor see toh]

"Tu pars toujours si tôt."

Type the word that should carry the push instead.
questions.why: The push moved to the word carrying the meaning. French does not do that at any speed. [tü par too-zhoor see TOH]

questions.q: Listen to the long sentence. How many pushes did you hear?

audio.clip: En hiver, les jours sont courts.

questions.why: Two groups, so two pushes. The number of pushes tells you how the speaker grouped it, which is information the written sentence does not always give you.

questions.q: Say it: "En été, il fait chaud, même la nuit."
questions.target: En été, il fait chaud, même la nuit.
questions.ipa: /ɑ̃.n‿e.te | il fɛ ʃo | mɛm la nɥi/
questions.why: Last one. Even all the way, a short breath at each break, and a hold at the end of every group. [ahⁿ-n‿ay-TAY | eel feh SHOH | mem la NWEE]

questions.q:
This reading is WRONG: [LUH sam-dee | zhuh lee | oo zhuh marsh]

"Le samedi, je lis, ou je marche."

Type the word that should carry the push instead.
questions.why: A three-group sentence needs three pushes. This one front-loads the first group and lets the rest run flat. [luh sam-DEE | zhuh LEE | oo zhuh MARSH]

sections.title: What you take with you

say.text: That is the sound system finished. One idea to keep.

sections.body: That is the last rule in the sound track, and it is the one that ties the others together. The silent letters, the elisions and the liaisons all decide which sounds are there. Rhythm decides how they are spaced. Even syllables, then one push at the end. Say that to yourself before you speak and most of the English will fall out of your French on its own.
points: Even syllables, then one push at the end.
The push is per group. A long sentence breathes several times, and each breath ends on a push.
Nothing gets louder. The final syllable is simply held a little longer.
Up is a question, down is a statement, and no word has to change.
Where you break a phrase can change what you said.

segments.text: Hi, I am Camille. This lesson is about the music of French, and the whole of it fits in one line. Even syllables, then one push at the end.
You already know the sounds. What we are fixing today is the shape they make together, because that is the part that still says English.
Il fait froid.
Three syllables, all the same length, and only the last one held. Say it with me.
Here is the whole rule, and I am going to say it the same way every time. Even syllables, then one push at the end.
English stretches the syllable it cares about and swallows the rest. French does neither. Nothing is swallowed, and the only thing marking the end is a slight hold.
Le chat dort.
Now longer. Six to eight syllables, still one group, so still one push at the very end. Listen for how flat the middle stays.
Il pleut beaucoup dehors.
L'air froid pique fort dehors.
Notice the push did not move to the important word. It does not care what the sentence is about.
Your turn without me leading. I will give you the English, you give me the French, and keep it flat until the last syllable.
Now a sentence that breaks in two. Two groups means two pushes: one at the end of each. Do not run them together.
J'ai trop froid ce matin, je reste sous les draps.

segments.expected: J'ai trop froid ce matin, je reste sous les draps.

segments.text: And one more, three groups this time. One sentence that breathes twice, not three sentences.

segments.expected: Le matin, je me lève, et je pars.

segments.text: One check. I am going to say this two ways, and only one of them is French.
If you heard the break after mange, you heard someone calling the children to the table. Without it, the children are the meal.
Three things to keep. Even syllables, then one push at the end.
The push is per group, not per sentence. A long sentence breathes several times and each breath ends on a hold.
And up is a question, down is a statement, with no word changing.
À bientôt.

lessons.title: Masterclass
lessons.intro: Nine lessons taught you five rules, one at a time. In real speech they fire together, on the same word, in a fixed order, and they interact: a letter one rule put to sleep is the letter another rule wakes. This lesson is the order they run in and the speed they have to run at, on sentences where two or three of them collide.

overview.titleEn: Masterclass: the whole sound system at once
overview.introFr: Neuf leçons vous ont appris cinq règles, une par une. Dans la vraie parole, elles agissent ensemble, sur le même mot, dans un ordre fixe. Cette leçon vous donne cet ordre et la vitesse qu'il exige, sur des phrases où deux ou trois règles se rencontrent.

sections.title: Five words, one at a time

say.text: You know every word in this call and every rule it needs. Watch what happens anyway.

beats.text: A phone call to a restaurant you have been to twenty times. No face to read, nothing to point at, and the other person is not slowing down for you.
You have one line to say and you have known every word in it for weeks. You have also learned every rule it needs. All five of them.

options.fr: On arrive à l'heure, comme d'habitude.

say.text: Five things. Every one is something you do out loud, at speed, on a sentence you have not seen.

goals.s: Find where a phrase breaks before you make a single decision about a letter, because nothing joins across a break.

goals.t: Run the joins in one pass
goals.s: Handle elision and liaison as one move rather than two, so an unseen phrase takes one scan instead of two.
Say nothing at the end of a word unless something actually woke it, and stop overcorrecting the ones that stay silent.
Say les hôtels and les héros correctly first time, and know why the page could not have told you which was which.

goals.s: Apply five rules to a sentence you have never read, at conversation pace, without stopping to work any of them out.

sections.title: One idea, then three steps
sections.hint: Swipe through. Nothing to answer yet.

say.text: Six cards. The first one is the whole lesson and the other five are it slowed down.

cards.head: French pronounces the phrase, not the word.
cards.body: French does not decide how a word sounds and then put words in a row. It builds a phrase group first, and decides what every letter inside it does afterwards.

cards.head: Group, join, push.
cards.body: Three steps, always in that order. Each one depends on the answer to the one before it, so running them out of order gives the wrong answer even when you know all five rules.

cards.head: Step one: group
cards.body: Where does the phrase break? Nothing joins across a break, so this decides which words are even allowed to touch. Get it wrong and every later step is wrong too.

cards.head: Step two: join
cards.body: Inside a group, and only inside it: a vowel meeting a vowel deletes the small word's vowel, and a sleeping consonant meeting a vowel wakes up. One move, not two.

cards.head: Step three: push
cards.body: One prominence per group, on its last syllable, wherever the joining ended up putting it. Not one push per word. That is the single loudest giveaway of an English speaker.

cards.head: And the rest stays silent
cards.body: Anything the joining did not touch keeps doing what it always did, which is nothing. Most letters at the ends of French words never move at all.

say.text: One phrase per card. Say each one and ask a single question: did you have to stop anywhere inside it?

check.q: Why can nothing join across the comma?

check.why: A break ends a group, and a join only ever happens inside one. That is why finding the break has to come first: it decides what the joining is even allowed to look at.

say.text: A group can end where nothing on the page says so. This is the one place that catches everybody.

rule.title: A noun subject closes its group
rule.body: A comma is not the only break. When a noun subject is followed by its verb, the group ends between them: les enfants arrivent has a Z at the front and silence in the middle. A pronoun subject does not, so ils arrivent joins.

cards.tip: Pronoun subject. It sits inside the same group as its verb, so the S wakes.
Noun subject. The group ends after enfants, and no join crosses the end of a group.
Determiner and noun, always one group. This join is never optional.

questions.q: How many pushes were in the first line?
questions.why: Two, because there are two groups. The push lands on matin and again on école, and nowhere in between.

questions.q: In the second line, which syllable was pushed?
questions.why: The last. One group means one push, and a French group always pushes its final syllable.

questions.q: A join moved a consonant onto the next word. What happened to the push?
questions.why: The push belongs to the last syllable of the group, and joining changes which syllable that is. It follows the sound, not the spelling.

sections.title: What happens when they meet
sections.hint: Five outcomes. Swipe through, then the drill.

say.text: Two words meet inside a group. There are only five things that can happen, and you know all five.

cards.label: Vowel meets vowel
cards.head: The small word loses its vowel
cards.body: Elision. ne and de both give way here, and neither is optional. This is the only one of the five that shows on the page.

cards.label: Sleeping consonant meets vowel
cards.head: The consonant wakes
cards.body: Liaison. The S of les says nothing in every other sentence you have ever read. Here it says Z, because a vowel needs it.

cards.label: Anything meets consonant
cards.head: Nothing happens at all
cards.body: The commonest outcome by a long way. No collision, nothing to fill, so every letter stays exactly as it was.

cards.label: Vowel meets vowel, nothing to give
cards.head: The gap simply stays
cards.body: a is not a small word that can drop a vowel and has no sleeping consonant to lend. So French leaves the two vowels side by side.

cards.label: And across a break
cards.head: None of it applies
cards.body: French pronounces the phrase, not the word. A group is what all four outcomes above happen inside, so a group edge switches every one of them off.

check.q: What do elision and liaison have in common?
opts: both fire when a vowel sound follows
check.why: They are one move with two outcomes. The trigger is identical: the next word starts on a vowel sound. Elision deletes a vowel, liaison wakes a consonant, and which one you get depends on what the first word ends in.

check.q: What decides whether a final consonant sounds?
opts: the first sound of the next word
check.why: Never the word itself. The same S in les is silent before a consonant and a Z before a vowel, and nothing about les changed between the two. The decision is made by what comes next, inside the same group.

rule.title: One H does nothing, and one H stops everything
rule.body: No H in French is pronounced, so neither kind makes a sound. What an h aspiré does is BLOCK, and it is the only thing in the language that stops both joins at once. les hôtels takes its Z and les héros does not.

cards.tip: H muet. The word opens on a vowel sound, so the plural S wakes as normal.
H aspiré. Same shape on the page, opposite behaviour, and a small gap instead of a Z.
H muet. An X wakes as a Z, exactly as an S would.
H aspiré. Both X stay silent and the gap is the only thing marking it.
H muet, so both sleeping T in this sentence wake up.
H aspiré. The same two T, and now neither of them says anything.

say.text: Seven ways this falls apart. Five of them are things you started doing because you learned a rule.

errors.wrong: les enfants-z-arrivent
errors.right: Les enfants arrivent.
errors.why: Overcorrection. Learning liaison makes people link everything, and a noun subject before its verb is a group edge that nothing crosses.

errors.wrong: les-z-héros
errors.right: les héros
errors.why: H aspiré blocks it. The H is silent in both kinds, so nothing you can see distinguishes them and this one has to be learned as a word.

errors.wrong: un bonn ami, with a hard N and a flat vowel
errors.right: un bon ami
errors.why: The vowel stays nasal AND the N links. Un-nasalising it to make room for the N gives away that you are working it out.

errors.wrong: On... arrive... à... l'heure.
errors.right: On arrive à l'heure.
errors.why: Every word right and no phrase. Applying the rules one word at a time is correct and far too slow to be speech.

errors.wrong: Le matin les enfants vont à l'école, with no stop
errors.right: Le matin, les enfants vont à l'école.
errors.why: One group where there should be two. Running a break over is the mirror of joining across one, and it costs the listener the structure.

errors.wrong: toutt, with the T said
errors.right: tout va bien
errors.why: Nothing woke that T. A consonant follows it, so it goes on doing what it does everywhere else, which is nothing.

errors.wrong: a push on every word
errors.right: one push per group
errors.why: English stresses words and French stresses groups. Pushing each word is the single loudest accent marker there is, more than any individual sound.

sections.title: Faster than you can decide

say.text: You know all of this. What is left is doing it in the time a conversation actually gives you.

sections.intro: The five rules are not the problem any more. The problem is that you are applying them one at a time, in order, consciously, and a conversation does not wait for that. French pronounces the phrase, not the word. So the thing to train is not another rule. It is the habit of taking in a whole group before your mouth starts, which is physical rather than intellectual, and it comes from doing rather than knowing.

targets.label: Read the group first
targets.sub: For any phrase you have not seen
steps: Cover the sentence and uncover only as far as the first break.
Read that group silently, all of it, before you make any sound.
Now say it, in one run, with one push at the end.
Uncover the next group and do the same. Never start a group you have not finished reading.

targets.label: The run-on
targets.sub: For a group with several joins in it
steps: Say the group deliberately too fast, faster than you can hesitate.
Notice that the joins survive and only the pauses die.
Slow back down to normal speed while keeping every join closed.
Repeat until the slow version has no more gaps than the fast one.

targets.label: Leave it alone
targets.sub: For the letters that must stay silent
steps: Say a phrase where nothing joins, and deliberately try to link it.
Hear how wrong the extra consonant sounds.
Say it correctly, and notice that correct feels like doing less.
Alternate the two until leaving a letter alone feels like a decision rather than a lapse.

closing.text: When you can read a group before your mouth starts, this lesson is done and so is the track.

say.text: Eight sentences you have not worked on, from earlier lessons. Count the groups before you look.

sections.title: A paragraph of all of it

say.text: Read it out loud, all the way through, before you look at a single question.

sections.text: Le matin, les enfants vont à l'école. On arrive à l'heure, comme d'habitude, parce que c'est un très bon quartier et tout est à côté. Après le dîner, on prend un verre d'eau et les autres attendent dans le petit hôtel en face. Ce sont mes amis, ils habitent en Angleterre depuis deux ans. Ils sont partis très tôt, sans nous attendre, et il n'a pas encore mangé. Quand on est en retard, tout le monde attend, et les héros de cette histoire sont les enfants.

glossary.note: The S wakes here and then goes straight back to sleep before attendent.
A consonant follows en, so the N stays inside the vowel.
The X of deux wakes as a Z. The S of depuis has a consonant after it and does not.
H aspiré, so no Z and a small gap, in a sentence with three other liaisons in it.

questions.q: Find every group boundary in the second sentence and say what marks each one.
questions.a: Two commas, and nothing else. Everything between them is one run: comme and habitude join, and c'est un très bon carries a T and then nothing before bon.

questions.q: The passage has « les autres attendent » and « les amis ». Why does one of them have two joins and the other one?
questions.a: les autres joins on a Z because autres opens on a vowel. autres attendent does not join, because a noun subject closes its group before its verb.

questions.q: Why is it « les héros » with a gap and « les enfants » with a Z, in the same sentence?
questions.a: héros is h aspiré and blocks the join. enfants opens on a vowel sound with nothing blocking, so the S of les wakes. Neither H nor E is pronounced.

questions.q: Count the silent final consonants in the last sentence, and say what would have woken any of them.
questions.a: Six: the D of quand does wake, but retard, attend, sont and enfants do not, because each is followed by a consonant, a break, or nothing at all.

questions.q: Read the third sentence aloud. How many times should you stop inside it?
questions.a: Once, at the comma. Everything after it runs together, including prend un and petit hôtel, which are joins you cannot see on the page.

say.text: Twelve cards. Answer each one out loud before you rate it.

cards.front: The one thing all five rules have in common
cards.back: French pronounces the phrase, not the word.

cards.front: The order the rules run in
What you decide first, on any sentence
cards.back: Where it breaks. Nothing joins across a break, so every other decision depends on this one.
The next word starting on a vowel SOUND, inside the same group. Never a vowel letter.

cards.front: The difference between elision and liaison
cards.back: What the first word ends in. A vowel is deleted; a sleeping consonant is woken. Same trigger, two outcomes.
Nothing. Silence is the default, and most final consonants never move.
On the last syllable of each group, after joining has decided which syllable that is.

cards.front: Two things that block both joins
cards.back: A phrase break, and an h aspiré. Nothing else blocks both.

cards.front: What blocks a liaison but not an elision
cards.back: A noun subject sitting in front of its verb. Les enfants arrivent, with silence in the middle.

cards.front: What a nasal N does before a vowel
cards.back: Both jobs at once. The vowel stays nasal and an N appears in front of the next word.

cards.front: Your guess for an unknown H word
cards.back: Muet. Most French H are, and nearly every aspiré one is a recent borrowing.

cards.front: Why you are still slow, if you are
cards.back: You are deciding word by word. Read the whole group before your mouth starts.

sections.title: Where you are

say.text: Before the exam, a second to see what nine lessons have actually added up to.

sections.body: Nine lessons taught you five rules, one at a time, and each of them made sense on its own. What you did not have until today is the order they run in and the speed they have to run at. Those are the only two things this lesson added, and between them they are the difference between reading French correctly and speaking it.

stats.v: A1, and none of this comes up again

say.text: Round one. Before anything else, where does the phrase break.

questions.q: Where does « Le matin, je bois mon café. » break?
questions.why: At the comma. That is one group and then another, and the push lands twice: once on matin and once at the end.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: The break is the only difference, and it changes who is being eaten. Two groups with a gap, against one group with a Z in it.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Ils arrivent has a Z in the middle, because a pronoun subject does not close a group. Les enfants arrivent has silence in the same place.

questions.q: Say it, and break where the comma is: In the morning, the children go to school.
questions.target: Le matin, les enfants vont à l'école.
questions.why: Two groups. Inside the second one, one join is made, one is refused and one is made again, all without slowing down.

questions.q: Type the word that ends the first group in « Le matin, les enfants vont à l'école. »
questions.why: matin sits right before the comma, so it carries the push and closes the group. Nothing after it can join back across that edge.

questions.q: A learner reads « Les enfants arrivent » with a Z before arrivent. Type the two words that DO join in that sentence.
questions.why: les and enfants sit inside one group, so they join. enfants and arrivent are on opposite sides of the subject boundary, so they never do.

say.text: Round two. Elision, and the one thing that stops it.

questions.q: Type it: I have no friends here.
questions.why: ne and de both lose their vowel. The S of pas stays silent because a D follows it, not a vowel.

questions.q: Type it: What are we waiting for?
questions.why: Two elisions turn four written words into four spoken syllables, and then the N of on links straight onto attend.

questions.q: A learner writes « Je ne ai pas de argent ». Fix both elisions.
questions.why: ne + ai and de + argent are both vowel collisions, and neither elision is optional. There is no slower French in which they stay whole.

questions.q: Say it: It is too early.
questions.why: C'est is one syllable. Putting the E of ce back is the single most common way to sound like you are reading rather than speaking.

questions.q: Why is there no elision before mangé in « Il n'a pas mangé »?
questions.why: A join only fires where the next word starts on a vowel sound. The M of mangé is a consonant, so nothing collides and nothing gives way.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Both open on the same elision and the same T. They part on the third join: bon lends an N and bel lends an L.

say.text: Round three. Liaison, and which letter actually wakes.

questions.q: In « un grand arbre », what sound does the D of grand make?
questions.why: A final D wakes as a T, never as a D. The liaison consonant is not always the letter you are looking at.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: The same D in both. It says T in front of a vowel and nothing in front of a consonant, and there is no other difference between them.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: The S of les sounds in one and not the other, and what decided it was the first sound of the word after it.

questions.q: Say it: We have two children.
questions.why: An S and an X, both silent as written, both saying Z here. Neither join may carry a pause in front of it.

questions.q: Say it: We are early.
questions.why: Three joins in four words. Said correctly it is five syllables with nothing at all between them.

questions.q: Type the linking consonant you hear in the middle of « ils ont ». One letter.
questions.why: The S of ils says Z. A liaison S is always voiced, which is why les amis is lay-z and never lay-s.

say.text: Round four. Most of it stays silent, and adding a join is as wrong as missing one.

questions.q: Tap the letter you do not say in this word.
questions.why: The final S is written and silent. There is no vowel after it inside this group, so nothing is there to wake it.

questions.q: How many audible consonants close the words in « Tout va bien »?
questions.why: None. The T of tout is asleep because a consonant follows it, and bien ends in a nasal vowel with no N after it.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Tout est carries a T in the middle and Tout va carries nothing. It is the same letter of the same word in both.

questions.q: Say it: They left very early.
questions.why: Five words, five silent endings, and no join available anywhere in it. Inventing one is the classic way to overcorrect.

questions.q: Type it: Everything is fine.
questions.why: Three short words, and the T you can see is one you must not say. Silence is the default the system falls back to.

questions.q: A learner writes « Il ont mangé » and cannot hear where the Z comes from. Fix the spelling.
questions.why: The plural S is the whole liaison. Drop it from the spelling and the Z you can hear has nothing left to come from.

say.text: Round five. The hard part, and nothing on the page will help you.

questions.q: Which of these blocks BOTH the elision and the liaison?
questions.why: hibou is h aspiré. It is the only thing in French that blocks both joins, and nothing in the spelling shows it.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: One has a Z and one has a small gap where the Z would have been. That gap is the only signal an h aspiré ever gives you.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: The X of deux says Z before an h muet and nothing before an h aspiré. Both of those words are spelled with an H.

questions.q: Say it: The little hero has left.
questions.why: Two sleeping T and both stay down. Waking the first one turns héros into a word French does not have.

questions.q: A learner writes « l'héros ». Fix it.
questions.why: h aspiré blocks the elision as well as the liaison. The article keeps its vowel even though the H makes no sound at all.

questions.q: Type the correct article plus noun for « hibou », the owl.
questions.why: hibou is h aspiré, so le keeps its E. When you genuinely do not know which H you have, guess muet: it is far more common.

say.text: Round six. The N that does two jobs at once.

questions.q: In « un bon ami », what happens to the vowel of bon?
opts: it stays nasal and an N is added
questions.why: The N does both jobs at once. The vowel still goes through the nose AND an N appears in front of ami, and neither is spent on the other.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Three syllables each, and only one of them has an audible N in the middle. The vowel of bon is nasal in both.

questions.q: Say it: in an instant.
questions.why: Four nasal vowels and two linking N in three words. Each N belongs to the syllable after it, not the one before.

questions.q: Say it: They have a child.
questions.why: Six spoken syllables out of four written words, with three joins holding them together and no pause available anywhere.

questions.q: Type it: my former flat.
questions.why: Two N link and four vowels stay nasal. The N you hear was never a separate letter you could have chosen to drop.

questions.q: A learner says « un bon copain » with an N before copain. Type the phrase where that N is correct.
questions.why: An N only surfaces where a vowel follows it. copain starts on a consonant, so there is nothing for the N to attach to.

say.text: Round seven. Every question here needs more than one rule.

questions.q: In « Il n'a pas encore mangé », what happens to ne and to pas?
opts: ne elides and the S of pas wakes
ne elides and pas stays silent
questions.why: One rule deletes a vowel and another wakes a consonant, three letters apart. Take encore out and only the second one stops.

questions.q: Say it: It is a former hotel.
questions.why: One elision and two liaisons, run together as a single unbroken word. Any pause inside it is the error.

questions.q: Say it: Have a large glass of water.
questions.why: The Z of prenez wakes and the D of grand does not, four words apart, and the same one thing decided both of them.

questions.q: Type it: That is a very good example.
questions.why: The S of très sits between two liaisons and makes none of its own, because bon opens on a consonant.

questions.q: Type it: We have had enough.
questions.why: Two joins, then two vowels side by side with nothing between them. a has no sleeping consonant to lend, so the gap stays.

questions.q: A learner reads « les héros » with a Z. Type the phrase from this lesson where les DOES take a Z before an H word.
questions.why: Both words open on a silent H and only one lets the join through. Nothing in the spelling could have told you which.

say.text: Last round. You know all of this. The only question left is whether you can do it in time.

questions.q: You meet a sentence you have never seen. What do you decide FIRST?
questions.why: Group first. Nothing joins across a break, so deciding a join before you know the groups can only ever be a guess.

questions.q: Say it: When we are late, everyone waits.
questions.target: Quand on est en retard, tout le monde attend.
questions.why: Four joins, one break and five nasal vowels. At conversation speed there is no room to decide any of it word by word.

questions.q: Say it: In the morning, the children go to school.
questions.target: Le matin, les enfants vont à l'école.
questions.why: All five rules in one line: a break, a join made, a join refused, a join made, and a push at the end of each group.

questions.q: Type it: We arrive on time, as usual.
accept: on arrive à l'heure, comme d'habitude
on arrive a lheure comme dhabitude
on arrive à l’heure, comme d’habitude
questions.answer: On arrive à l'heure, comme d'habitude.
questions.why: Two elisions, one liaison and one slide, split across a break. Every one of them is compulsory.

questions.q: Type the three steps of the system, in order, separated by commas.
questions.why: Group decides where nothing may cross. Join fires inside each group and only there. Push lands on the last syllable of each one.

questions.q: A learner reads « Les enfants arrivent » as three separate words with a pause between each. Type what they should have joined.
questions.why: One join, and only one. The pause between enfants and arrivent is correct. The pause between les and enfants is not.

sections.title: What you take with you

say.text: That is the track. Five things worth keeping, and the first one contains the other four.

sections.body: An hour ago you knew five rules and a person on a telephone waited for you to finish a sentence you thought you had started. Nothing was wrong with the words. What was missing was the group, and the order, and the speed. You now read a phrase before you speak it, which is the only version of this that is any use in a conversation, and it is the last thing the sons track had to give you.
points: French pronounces the phrase, not the word. Every rule you have learned is a consequence of that, and none of them is a separate decision.
Group, join, push. Group first, because nothing joins across a break. Then join, inside each group only. Then push, on the last syllable of each one.
A join fires on a vowel SOUND, not a vowel letter. Elision deletes a vowel and liaison wakes a consonant, and the trigger for both is identical.
Everything the joining did not touch stays silent, which is most of it. Adding a link French does not make is as wrong as missing one it does.
Two things block both joins: a phrase break and an h aspiré. A noun subject in front of its verb blocks the liaison alone, and nothing on the page shows any of them.

acts.milestone: The gap, named.

acts.title: Group it
acts.milestone: Where the phrase ends.

acts.title: Join it
acts.milestone: Both joins, one move.

acts.title: Where the rules fight
acts.milestone: The blockers, beaten.

acts.milestone: Sons track complete.

lessons.reframe: French pronounces the phrase, not the word.

errorTriggers.description: Joins across a phrase break, or fails to break at all and runs two groups into one.
Leaves a compulsory elision or liaison unmade: je aime, les_amis with a gap.
Makes a join French forbids: a Z into les héros, or a link from a noun subject to its verb.
Decides from the letter rather than the sound: reads an H, or says an N after a nasal vowel.
Applies the rules one word at a time, correctly but far too slowly to be speech.

drills.title: Find the edge
drills.coach: Six phrases. Say each one out loud and decide where, if anywhere, you had to stop.

drills.title: One more edge
drills.q: Which of these is TWO groups rather than one?
drills.why: The comma is a real break. The other three run straight through with no place to stop inside them.

drills.title: Make the join
drills.coach: Six phrases, every one of them with a compulsory join in it. Write what the join actually sounds like.

drills.title: Once more
drills.q: Type the linking sound in « nous avons ». One letter.
drills.why: The S of nous wakes as a Z, because avons opens on a vowel and the two words are inside one group.
drills.coach: Just the one.

drills.title: Join, or leave it
drills.coach: Three of these join and three do not. Two are blocked by an H and one by the edge of a group.

drills.title: The gap
drills.q: Which one did you hear?
drills.why: les hôtels runs straight through on a Z. les héros leaves a small gap where an h aspiré blocked it.

drills.title: The sound, not the letter
drills.coach: Four pairs. In each one the spelling gives you nothing, so listen and then decide.

drills.title: One decision
drills.q: You meet a new word starting with H and have to guess. Which way?
drills.why: Most French H are muet, and nearly every aspiré one is a recent borrowing. Muet is the better guess by a long way.

drills.title: Faster than you can decide
drills.coach: Five sentences. Say each one faster than you can work it out. The rules survive speed; the hesitation does not.

drills.title: At speed, once
drills.q: Say « Quand on est en retard, tout le monde attend » with one stop, at the comma, and nowhere else.
drills.why: Four joins and one break. If you can place the single stop correctly at speed, the system is running on its own.

sheets.title: The whole sound system, on one page

sections.title: The order, and what each step decides
rows: Which words are allowed to touch each other at all.
Does the next word start on a vowel sound?
Elision if a vowel would collide, liaison if a sleeping consonant can fill the gap.
Where the one prominence lands, after the joining has moved things.
Did anything above touch this letter?
If not, it stays silent. Most letters at the ends of words never move.

sections.title: What blocks a join
rows: A noun subject before its verb
le héros, les héros, le hibou
A consonant on the next word
et un, never with a T

sections.title: Which letter wakes as which sound
rows: les amis, deux heures, chez elle
neuf ans, neuf heures, and nowhere else

sheets.title: The twelve pairs, in full
contains: Every minimal pair this lesson teaches

sections.title: Same letters, two behaviours
rows: A vowel against a consonant, and the D says T.
A vowel against a consonant, and the vowel stays nasal in both.
H muet against h aspiré. Nothing on the page shows it.
A vowel against a consonant, and the Z is the only audible difference.
A pronoun subject against a noun subject.
H muet against h aspiré, twice in one sentence.
One word removed, and the Z goes with it.
Ils sont partis très tôt, sans nous attendre.
A sixth word arrives and one S wakes.

sections.title: What every pair on this page has in common
points: The two halves are spelled the same up to the point where they differ.
Nothing in the spelling of the differing word tells you which way it goes.
The decision is always made by the first SOUND of the next word, or by a group edge.
That is why the ear has to lead here, and why every one of these has a recording.

phraseGroup.title: The unit French actually pronounces
phraseGroup.body: English decides how a word sounds and then puts words in a row. French does not. It builds a GROUP first, a short run of syllables said in one flow with a single push at the end, and only then decides what each letter inside it does. That is why the same word changes: petit before a consonant and petit before a vowel are the same word in two different groups, and the group is what chose. Everything in this lesson follows from it. A letter goes silent because nothing in its group needs it. A letter comes back because the next sound in the group needs a consonant. A vowel is deleted because the group will not carry two vowels in a row. Find the group before you decide anything else, because nothing joins across the edge of one.

examples.note: the subject closes its group, so the second S stays down
two groups, one Z inside each
a break, then three joins inside one group

pipeline.title: The order the rules run in
pipeline.body: The five rules are not five decisions you make at once. They are a sequence, and each step depends on the one before it. FIRST group: find where the phrase breaks, because nothing joins across a break and getting this wrong makes every later step wrong. THEN join, inside each group and only inside it: two vowels meeting means the small word loses its vowel, and a sleeping consonant in front of a vowel wakes up. Everything the joining did not touch stays exactly as silent as it was. THEN push: one prominence per group, on its last syllable, wherever the joining ended up putting that syllable. Run it in that order and a sentence you have never seen comes out right the first time.

examples.note: break, then join, then two pushes
four joins inside two groups
the second group runs seven syllables with no stop

join.title: Elision and liaison are one operation
join.body: You met these as two lessons and they are one move. Both fire at exactly the same moment, when a word is about to run into a vowel sound, and both exist to stop the group stumbling. Elision handles the case where the first word ENDS in a vowel: the vowel goes and an apostrophe marks the spot. Liaison handles the case where the first word ends in a silent consonant: the consonant comes back and attaches to the front of the next word. One deletes, one adds, and neither is optional where it applies. Thinking of them as one thing is what lets you scan a phrase once instead of twice, and speed is the whole difficulty at this stage.

examples.note: an elision and two liaisons in four words
the elision and the liaison land two words apart
two elisions, and then a gap nothing can join

sleeping.title: Silent, or silent for now
sleeping.body: A final consonant in French is written and not said, which is what sons.06 called silent unless there is a reason. This lesson is where the reason arrives. The letter is not absent, it is asleep, and a vowel sound immediately after it in the same group wakes it. The S of les says nothing in les copains and says a Z in les amis. The T of petit says nothing in un petit chien and says a T in un petit ami. Nothing about the word changed. What changed is what came next. So there is no such thing as a permanently silent final consonant: there are letters that happen to have nothing after them, and letters that do.

examples.note: awake
asleep, same letter
a D that wakes up as a T

hAspire.title: The one thing that blocks both joins
hAspire.body: Every H in French is silent, so the H itself never makes a sound. What some of them do is BLOCK. An h muet does nothing at all: the word behaves as if the H were not written, so elision and liaison both fire normally. An h aspiré blocks both of them, and it is the only thing in the language that does. les hôtels links and les héros does not; l'homme contracts and le hibou does not. Out loud the block leaves a small gap where the join would have been, and that gap is the only signal there is. Nothing in the spelling separates the two kinds, so each aspiré word is learned with its article, the way a noun is learned with its gender. When you genuinely do not know, guess muet: it is far more common.

examples.note: h muet, so the join fires
h aspiré, so it does not
both joins in the sentence blocked

nasalN.title: The N that keeps its vowel and still links
nasalN.body: A nasal vowel is a vowel with an N or an M written after it that is not a separate sound: bon is one syllable, not two, and the N is inside the vowel rather than after it. The question this lesson answers is what happens when a vowel follows. The answer is that the N does both jobs at once. In un bon ami the vowel of bon is still nasal AND an N appears in front of ami, and the N is not spent on either job. That is why bon ami has three syllables and bon copain has three too, but only one of them has an audible N in the middle. The N was always there. It only becomes audible when the next sound needs a consonant.

examples.note: nasal kept, N heard
nasal kept, no N anywhere
four nasal vowels, two linking N

notation.title: Four marks, and what each one claims
notation.body: This lesson brings together the notation of five earlier ones and adds nothing. A tie, as in lay-z‿a-MEE, means a consonant has attached to the FOLLOWING syllable, which is where it is really said. A vertical bar means a phrase break: nothing joins across it. CAPITALS mark the pushed syllable, always the last one in its group. A small raised n, as in bohⁿ, means the vowel goes through the nose and does NOT mean you should say an N. IPA sits between slashes and is exact; the respelling sits between brackets and is a reading aid. When the two disagree, trust the IPA.

examples.note: all four marks in one line
three ties and four raised n

recorded.desc: The phone-call break beat. ONE VOICE, ONE SPEED, ONE TAKE, back to back: first the word-by-word reading with a real pause between each of the five words, then the correct reading with two groups and a single stop at the comma. The two takes must be the same speaker at the same tempo, because the ONLY difference being taught is where the stops are, and a listener cannot judge that across two recordings.

The grouping contrast, and the recording this lesson depends on most after rec-pairs. Ten phrases: five that run as one group (On est en avance, C'est un ancien hôtel, Ils ont un enfant, en un instant, Tout est prêt) and five with one internal break. CRITICAL: the break must be a real pause of roughly 200ms plus a pitch reset, not merely a lengthened syllable, and every phrase must be one voice at one speed in one take. Include « On mange, les enfants » and « On mange les enfants » as an adjacent pair: the break is the only difference and device TTS renders it inconsistently, so this pair is unusable until it is recorded.

The subject/verb block. Six phrases in three adjacent pairs: Ils arrivent en retard against Les enfants arrivent, les amis against Mes amis parlent bien, Un ami arrive against les autres attendent. CRITICAL: one voice, one speed, one take per pair. The blocked side needs a genuine small gap where the Z would have been, not a glottal stop and not a lengthened vowel.

Five sentences read for PROMINENCE rather than for words, at normal pace plus a 0.65 pass. One push per group, on its final syllable, and no secondary stress anywhere. At the slow speed the group structure must survive: slowing down is not permission to push every word, and a slow take with word-level stress teaches the exact error the lesson exists to remove.

The ten multi-join phrases from mission 8, isolated, 900ms gaps, normal and 0.65. Each one must be a single unbroken run with no internal pause whatsoever: these are the reference for what a fully joined group sounds like, so they have to be flawless on that one point. At 0.65 the joins must STAY joined.

The twelve minimal pairs, and the single most important recording in the lesson. les amis / les copains, un petit ami / un petit chien, un grand arbre / un grand parc, un bon ami / un bon copain, les hôtels / les héros, deux heures / deux hiboux, ils ont / ils sont, Tout est prêt / Tout va bien, and the four sentence pairs. CRITICAL: each pair must be the SAME voice at the SAME speed in ONE take. The difference inside a pair is a single consonant or a gap of about 120ms, and a listener cannot judge either across two takes. Two takes at different tempos makes the pair uncomparable and the mission teaches nothing.

The h muet against h aspiré contrast, in sentence frames rather than isolated words. les hôtels / les héros, deux heures / deux hiboux, Le petit hôtel est ouvert / Le petit héros est parti. CRITICAL: one voice, one speed, one take per pair. The aspiré side needs a real, audible, deliberate gap rather than a glottal stop, because that gap is the only signal the learner is ever given and a glottal stop is a different sound teaching a different thing.

The nasal N pairs: un bon ami / un bon copain, mon ancien appartement, en un instant, un petit chien, Ils ont un enfant. CRITICAL: one voice, one speed, one take per pair, and the vowel of bon must stay AUDIBLY nasal in both halves. A take that de-nasalises it before ami teaches the opposite of the mission, and it is the single easiest thing for a speaker to do by accident when concentrating on the N.

The ten dictation sentences, normal speed only, natural connected delivery. No exaggerated separation between words: the learner is being asked to hear a joined group and write it back as separate words with the right silent letters, and a hyper-articulated take does that job for them.

The six-sentence reading passage, one take at natural conversational pace, plus per-sentence stems for tap-to-replay, plus the eight listening-mission sentences. The les héros instance must carry its blocked gap audibly, since a comprehension question turns on it, and the breaks must be real pauses because another question asks the learner to count them.

segments.text: I am Camille. This is the last lesson in the sound track, and it does not teach you a new rule.
You have five already. What you have never done is run all five at once, on a sentence you have not seen, at the speed a conversation actually goes.
On commence.
One idea first, and everything else follows from it. French does not pronounce words. It pronounces phrases.
les copains
les amis
Same S, same word. It is silent in the first and a Z in the second, and nothing about les changed. What changed is what came after it.
So there is an order. Group, join, push. Find where the phrase breaks first, because nothing joins across a break.
Le matin, les enfants vont à l'école.
Two groups. Inside the second one, les and enfants join, enfants and vont do not, and vont and à join again.
Then the push, once at the end of each group. Not once per word.
Now the part that decides everything. Listen to these two and tell me which one has an N in the middle.
un bon ami
un bon copain
The first one. And notice the vowel of bon stayed nasal in both: the N did two jobs at once rather than choosing one.
Your turn, and read the whole group before you start. Say: it is a former hotel.
Again, and this one has a break in it. When we are late, everyone waits.

segments.expected: Quand on est en retard, tout le monde attend.

segments.text: One trap before we finish. Two H words, both silent, and only one of them lets the join through. Which of these is correct?
les héros
les héros, with a small gap and no Z. Compare les hôtels, which is spelled the same way and joins.
Three things to keep. French pronounces the phrase, not the word. Group, join, push, always in that order.
And everything the joining did not touch stays silent, which is most of it. That is the whole sound system, and that is the track.
Bravo, et à bientôt.

lessons.title: Les salutations
lessons.intro: The first word you say in France decides how the rest of the conversation goes. This lesson is that word, the four versions of it, and everything that has to follow it.

say.text: Watch what happens. You are polite by every rule you have been taught, and it still goes wrong.

beats.text: Four days in Lyon. You have found a bakery you like.
You rehearsed this. You know the word, and you remember the please.

beats.prompt: What comes out of your mouth first?

options.en: the order, politely
the greeting, first

followUp.works: Yes. The order can wait three seconds. The greeting cannot.
followUp.breaks: That is the instinct every English speaker brings. Watch what it does.

beats.en: (the order, with no greeting in front of it)

beats.speaker: The baker
beats.en: (She reaches for the baguette without looking up.)
beats.stage: The warmth goes out of the room.

beats.heading: You skipped bonjour
beats.body: French does not work like English here. The greeting is what makes you a person in the room rather than a customer at a counter.

right.fr: Bonjour madame. Une baguette, s’il vous plaît.
right.ipa: /bɔ̃.ʒuʁ ma.dam yn ba.ɡɛt sil vu plɛ/

beats.coach: Same words, four syllables earlier. That is the whole difference.

beats.speaker: The baker
beats.stage: She is already reaching for your baguette.

beats.text: Four days of being served. One word, and you are a regular.

closing.text: Bonjour is the price of entry. You pay it first, every time, and then the conversation can start.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Bonjour is the price of entry. By the end of this lesson you will pay it without thinking, and you will know which version to use.

goals.s: Greet correctly on the way in, whatever time it is and whoever is behind the counter.
Decide how close you are before you speak, and know why the safe answer is the safe answer.
Reply to merci, to ça va, and to an introduction, without freezing.
Close a conversation the way French closes it, with a goodbye and a wish.

sections.title: Before Any Word, a Choice
sections.say: French makes you decide something English lets you leave vague. Here is the decision.

cards.label: The fork
cards.head: Two settings, one language
cards.body: English says "you" to a child and to a judge. French makes you pick. The choice happens before the sentence starts, and it shows in every word after it.

cards.label: Distance
cards.head: vous
cards.body: Strangers, anyone older, anyone serving you, anyone at work, and any group. This is the setting French leaves on by default.

cards.label: Closeness
cards.head: tu
cards.body: Friends, family, children, and people your own age once you have been invited. Until somebody offers it, staying on vous is not distant, it is correct.

sections.title: When to Say What
sections.say: Bonjour is the price of entry. The only question is which version the clock is asking for. Tap any row.

detail.title: Bonjour
detail.body: The default, and the one that is never wrong before evening. Say it to shopkeepers, neighbours, colleagues, strangers in a lift. Add madame or monsieur and it warms up further. There is no time of day too early for it.

detail.title: Bonsoir
detail.body: Swaps in for bonjour once the light has gone, roughly from six. It is a greeting for ARRIVING, not for leaving. Walking into a restaurant at eight, this is your word.

detail.title: Salut
detail.body: Works coming and going, which no other greeting here does. It belongs strictly to people you tutoie. Said to a shopkeeper it lands as over-familiar rather than friendly.

cells: On the phone, and nowhere else

detail.title: Allô
detail.body: A telephone word only. It is how you answer a call and how you check the line is still alive. Say it face to face and it reads as a joke.

detail.title: Bonne journée
detail.body: A wish for the person LEAVING, so it closes a conversation rather than opening one. The standard sign-off from a shop before evening, usually straight after au revoir.

detail.title: Bonne soirée
detail.body: The evening version of bonne journée, and the one most often confused with bonsoir. Bonsoir is hello. Bonne soirée is goodbye. Same part of the day, opposite doors.

detail.title: Bonne nuit
detail.body: Only when sleep is next. It is what you say to a child at bedtime or to a housemate on the stairs, not what you say leaving a dinner. For that you want bonne soirée.

sections.title: Three Traps
sections.say: Three mistakes that every English speaker makes, in the same order, in their first week.

errors.wrong: Walking in and saying « Une baguette, s’il vous plaît. »
errors.right: Walking in and saying « Bonjour madame. »
errors.why: Bonjour is the price of entry. The please does not cover it, because please softens a request and the problem is that you made a request at all before saying hello.

errors.wrong: Saying « Bonne nuit » as you leave a dinner party.
errors.right: Saying « Bonne soirée » as you leave a dinner party.
errors.why: Bonne nuit means sleep well. Used on the doorstep at ten it sounds like you are putting your hosts to bed. Bonne soirée is the one that wishes them a good rest of their evening.

errors.wrong: Opening with « Salut ! » to the person behind a counter.
errors.right: Opening with « Bonjour ! » to the person behind a counter.
errors.why: Salut is reserved for people you tutoie. To a stranger it reads as over-familiar, which lands worse than being too formal ever does.

sections.title: Two Doors, Same Street
sections.say: Two exchanges, thirty seconds apart, on the same street. Listen for what changes.

lines.fr: Bonjour madame. Comment allez-vous ?
lines.en: Hello madam. How are you?

lines.fr: Très bien, merci. Et vous ?
lines.en: Very well, thank you. And you?

lines.fr: Salut Léa ! Ça va ?
lines.en: Hi Léa! How’s it going?

lines.fr: Ça va bien, merci, et toi ?
lines.en: I’m good, thanks, and you?

questions.q: You walk into a shop at ten in the morning. What is the first thing out of your mouth?
questions.why: Bonjour covers every waking hour until dark, and going in it is never the wrong choice.

questions.q: In the first exchange, which word tells you they are on vous?
questions.why: Allez-vous is the vous form of the verb. Madame is a good clue but it is the verb that settles it.

questions.q: Someone says merci to you. What do you say back?
questions.why: De rien is the everyday reply, literally "of nothing". Saying merci back leaves the thanks unanswered.

sections.title: The Same Thing, Twice
sections.say: Five ideas, each in both forms. The meaning does not change. The distance does.

detail.title: How are you?
detail.body: The vous form is what you say to anyone you have just met. The tu form is for friends. Both are more formal than ça va, which is the version you will hear most.

rows.say: Comment vous appelez-vous ? Comment tu t’appelles ?

detail.title: What is your name?
detail.body: The vous form sounds long because it is: the verb takes vous twice. Nobody shortens it. The tu form is what you will use with anyone your own age.

rows.say: S’il vous plaît. S’il te plaît.

detail.title: Please
detail.body: One word changes and the rest stays. This is the pair you will use most often, and the one where the wrong form is most noticeable, because please turns up in every transaction.

detail.title: And you?
detail.body: Two syllables that turn an answer back into a conversation. French expects it: answering ça va and stopping there reads as closing the exchange down.

rows.say: Je vous remercie. Je te remercie.

detail.title: I thank you
detail.body: A step up from merci, for when someone has genuinely done something for you. The vous form is what you would write at the end of an email.

sections.title: One Phrase, Three Jobs
sections.say: Ça va is the most useful two words in the language, and it does three different jobs.

cards.label: Question
cards.head: Asking
cards.body: Rising tone at the end and it is a question. It works with anyone you would tutoie, and with almost anyone once the greeting is out of the way.

cards.label: Answer
cards.head: Answering
cards.body: Flat tone and it is an answer. Add merci and it is complete. Then hand it back with et toi, or et vous, or the exchange stops with you.

cards.label: Frankly
cards.head: Not great
cards.body: French does not require you to be fine. This is the accepted way of saying you are not, without making it a conversation.

sections.title: Giving Your Name
sections.say: Three ways to say who you are, and the one word you reply with when somebody tells you who they are.

sections.title: A Morning in the Building
sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Tap any word you do not know.
sections.text:
It is eight in the morning. Claire goes down the stairs. She meets madame Blanc.

« Bonjour madame. Comment allez-vous ? »
« Très bien, merci. Et vous ? »
« Ça va bien, merci. »

Out in the street, Claire sees Léa, a friend.

« Salut Léa ! Ça va ? »
« Ça va bien, merci, et toi ? »
« Comme ci, comme ça. À demain ! »
« À demain. Bonne journée ! »

glossary.note: The vous form. Comment allez-vous is the full, polite "how are you".
Très bien is the standard step up from plain bien.
The tu form after et. Vous would give et vous instead.
À demain names the day you will next meet.
The stretch of daylight, not the date. Bonne journée wishes you the rest of it.

questions.q: Why does Claire say vous to madame Blanc and tu to Léa?
questions.a: Madame Blanc is a neighbour she does not know well; Léa is a friend.

questions.q: Which greeting does Claire use twice, and which one only once?
questions.a: She uses ça va with both. Bonjour is only for madame Blanc, and salut only for Léa.

questions.q: What does Claire wish Léa at the end?
questions.a: Bonne journée, a good day, because it is still morning.

cards.back: Et vous ? or et toi ? Handing it back is expected.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have met the expressions, watched a scene, read a passage, spelled the sentences that are hard to spell and said the core phrases out loud. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Four rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one.

rounds.label: Walking in
rounds.say: The first three seconds.

questions.q: You walk into a small shop in Lyon. What comes out of your mouth first?
questions.why: Bonjour is the price of entry. The other three all skip it, and the please in option three does not buy it back.

questions.q: It is seven in the evening and you are arriving at a dinner. Which one?
questions.why: Bonsoir is the greeting for arriving after dark. Bonne soirée wishes someone a good evening as they leave.

questions.q: Bonne nuit belongs where?
opts: Arriving at a party after dark
Leaving someone who is going to bed
Greeting a shopkeeper in the evening
questions.why: It means sleep well. Anywhere else it sounds like you are sending the other person to bed.

questions.q: Write the greeting you use on the phone, and only on the phone.
questions.why: Allô is a telephone word. Face to face it reads as a joke.

questions.q: Listen. Which greeting is it?
questions.why: Bonsoir and bonne soirée sound close and mean opposite things. Bonsoir is hello, bonne soirée is goodbye.

questions.q: Fix this. It is eight in the evening and you are walking into a restaurant: « Bonne soirée ! »
questions.why: Bonne soirée is a wish for someone on their way out. Coming in, you want bonsoir.

rounds.label: How close are you?
rounds.say: The choice you make before you speak.

questions.q: The baker is about sixty and you have never met. Which?
questions.why: A stranger behind a counter takes vous, and allez-vous is the vous form.

questions.q: Your friend’s eight-year-old asks your name. You answer, then ask back. Which?
questions.why: A child takes tu, and et toi is the tu form of and you.

questions.q: Listen. Which form did you hear?
questions.why: Te against vous is the whole difference, and it is one syllable. This is the pair you will hear most often.

questions.q: You are not sure which form to use. What is the safe move?
opts: Use vous and wait to be invited to tu
questions.why: Being too formal is invisible. Being too familiar is not. The invitation to tu is a real moment and it will come.

questions.q: Rewrite this for a friend: « S’il vous plaît »
questions.why: One word swaps and the rest holds. Vous becomes te, not toi, because it is the object of the verb.

questions.q: Salut works for…
opts: hello and goodbye, with people you tutoie
questions.why: It is the only greeting here that runs both ways, and the only one restricted by register rather than by the clock.

rounds.label: Please, thank you, sorry
rounds.say: The half of politeness that gets left out.

questions.q: Someone thanks you. Write the everyday reply.
questions.why: De rien is the everyday you are welcome. Je vous en prie is the same move one register up and is accepted here. Answering merci with merci leaves the thanks hanging.

questions.q: You want to interrupt a stranger to ask directions. You open with:
questions.why: Excusez-moi is the vous form and the one for stopping someone you do not know. Pardon works too, and is shorter.

questions.q: Je vous en prie is…
opts: a more formal way of saying de rien
a way of saying thank you
questions.why: It is you are welcome, one register up. You will hear it from anyone serving you.

questions.q: Say it out loud: thank you very much.
questions.why: The final p of beaucoup is silent, and the word ends on an ou that stays rounded.

questions.q: You have just been introduced to someone. One word.
questions.why: Both spellings are accepted here because both are correct. Which one is yours depends on who is speaking.

questions.q: A woman is writing her own name card. Which spelling of "pleased to meet you" is hers?
questions.why: The extra e agrees with her. It changes nothing about how the word sounds.

rounds.label: On the way out
rounds.say: Closing it properly.

questions.q: You are leaving a shop at eleven in the morning. Write what comes after au revoir.
questions.why: Bonne journée wishes the rest of the day. It is the standard sign-off from any shop before evening.

questions.q: You are leaving a restaurant at ten at night. After au revoir:
questions.why: Bonne soirée is the evening version. Bonne nuit would suggest they are going to bed.

questions.q: You will see this person tomorrow. Write the goodbye that says so.
questions.why: À demain names the day. À bientôt, à plus tard and à la prochaine are all vaguer, and all correct when you do not know when.

questions.q: Listen. Which goodbye is it?
questions.why: À bientôt is soon without saying when. À plus tard means later the same day.

questions.q: Say it out loud, the way you would leaving a bakery.
questions.why: Said as one movement, not two sentences. The pause after au revoir is shorter than English wants it to be.

questions.q: The single move that changes how a French shop treats you:
opts: Greeting before you ask for anything
questions.why: This is the whole lesson in one line, and it is the one thing you can test tomorrow morning.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Six things you did not have this morning.
sections.body: You can walk into a shop in France and be treated as a person rather than a transaction. That is not a small thing, and it is almost entirely one word said at the right moment. Everything else in this lesson hangs off it.
points: Bonjour is the price of entry. Greet first, ask second, every single time.
Bonjour until dark, bonsoir after it, salut only with people you tutoie.
Bonsoir is hello and bonne soirée is goodbye, and they sound almost the same.
vous with anyone you do not know, and wait to be invited to tu.
When someone says merci, you say de rien. Half of politeness is the reply.
Answer ça va and hand it straight back with et vous ? or et toi ?

grammarIntroduced: The tu / vous distinction and when each is required
Gendered agreement on a bare adjective: enchanté / enchantée, désolé / désolée

drills.title: Greeting first, request second

drills.title: One more time

drills.why: Greeting, then request. The other two both start the transaction before you have said hello.

drills.title: Sort by the clock

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Nine in the evening, walking into a friend’s flat for dinner.
drills.why: You are arriving, so you need a greeting. The other two are both wishes for someone leaving.

drills.title: Which form is this?
drills.coach: Look for the pronoun. Te, toi and tu on one side; vous on the other. Salut has no pronoun and belongs to tu anyway.

drills.title: One more time

drills.why: A stranger serving you takes vous. Et tu is not a form anyone uses.

drills.title: The other half of politeness
drills.coach: They say the left. You say the right. Say it before you flip.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You hold a door. They say merci. You say…
drills.why: De rien closes the exchange. Merci back leaves it open, and pardon apologises for something that did not happen.

sheets.title: tu / vous, the full table
contains: Every paired form in this lesson
How the invitation to tu happens

sections.title: Who takes which
sections.body: vous: anyone you have not met, anyone older, anyone serving you, anyone at work above or beside you, teachers, officials, and every group of two or more people regardless of how well you know them. tu: friends, family, children, animals, and colleagues your own age once the offer has been made. The offer is a real moment with its own verb, on se tutoie, and it comes from the older or more senior person. Until then vous is not cold, it is simply correct, and nobody has ever been offended by it.
