sections.title: What to do with this
sections.body: Do not memorise the second table. It is here because a sheet should answer a question you actually have, which is usually about one specific word you are holding, and the fourteen endings on it cover between six and forty-one nouns each. The ten in the first table are the ones worth carrying in your head, and they cover about one gendered noun in five. For the other four in five there is nothing to work out, so the effort belongs on storing the article with the word rather than on a longer table. The floor for anything written down here is ninety percent: two endings that just miss it, -elle and -ie, are deliberately absent rather than shown with a warning, because a rule you half trust is what stops you looking a word up.

sheets.title: The nouns that hide their article

rows.v: un escalier, the staircase
un ordinateur, the computer
un appartement, the apartment
un enfant, the child
un avion, the plane
un oignon, the onion
une armoire, the wardrobe
une eau, the water
une école, the school
une oreille, the ear
une épaule, the shoulder
une huile, the oil

sections.title: How to check a new one
sections.body: There are more than two hundred of these in this app and no list will cover the ones you meet outside it, so the sheet is a worked set rather than a reference. The method is the useful part. Un and une do not elide in front of a vowel, so say the noun to yourself with each of them and one will sound wrong. If neither does, the word is genuinely new and the article has to be looked up, which takes five seconds now and saves the guess you would otherwise make at a counter. The endings help here more than anywhere else, because a noun beginning with a vowel is exactly the case where the front of the word tells you nothing and the back of it may still tell you everything.

pair.title: Why a noun on its own is only half a word
pair.body: A French noun is stored with the word in front of it. Armoire is something you can look up. Une armoire is something you can use, because the choice between un and une is made before you have finished the first syllable and there is no time to work it out mid-sentence. This is not a convention this lesson invented: nearly every noun in this app already carries its article, and a card that shows you the bare noun has quietly taught you to store it bare.

examples.note: The wardrobe, stored the way you will need it.
Water, where the article has been deleted and you still have to know it.

endings.title: The part you can work out
endings.body: Ten endings in French tell you the article, and across the nouns they cover they are right about ninety-seven times in a hundred. Five point to un: -ier, -ment, -et, -eau, -age. Five point to une: -tion, -ure, -ette, -ine, -ise. That is roughly one noun in six. It is a much smaller rule than most courses imply and it is a much better one, because the endings people usually teach are close to a coin toss.

examples.note: A board, and the ending says un before you know the word.
A question, where -tion has never once been wrong here.

finalE.title: The rule you were given, measured
finalE.body: Nouns ending in e are feminine is the first rule most beginners are handed, and over the eight hundred and seventy-one such nouns in this app it is right seven times in ten. Applied confidently it makes you wrong about one noun in three, which is often enough to sound wrong in every second sentence and rarely enough that you never stop trusting it. Le livre, le fromage, le téléphone and le frère all end in e. Keep the rule as a lean, never as a decision.

examples.note: Ends in e, takes le. So does its opposite number, la table.
Ends in e, takes la. Nothing on either card tells you which.

hidden.title: The two hundred nouns that tell you nothing
hidden.body: In front of a vowel, un stays un and une stays une, but le and la both shrink to l apostrophe. More than two hundred nouns in this app show up that way, and the card you learn them from carries no information about gender at all. L’armoire is feminine, l’escalier is masculine, and nothing you can see says so. The fix is a habit rather than a rule: the moment you meet l apostrophe, ask which one it really is, because nothing later will ask for you.

examples.note: Feminine, and the card does not say so.
Masculine, and the card does not say that either.

storage.term: work it out or store it
storage.title: Which of the two you are doing
storage.body: About one noun in six gives its article away through its ending. The rest do not, and no amount of looking at them will change that, so the strategy that survives contact with real French is: work it out where the ending lets you, and store the article with the word everywhere else. That is uncomfortable to be told and it is what actually works. The alternative is a learner who has memorised a table and still stops mid-sentence, which is the failure this lesson exists to stop.

examples.note: Worked out: -age points at un.
Stored: no ending in this lesson reaches it, and none ever will.

agreement.title: Why the article is worth the effort now
agreement.body: Gender is not a label on a noun, it is a choice that spreads. The article you pick is the same choice that decides le or la in the next lesson, du or de la after that, and the ending of every adjective you ever attach to the noun. Get the article stored once and all of those come free. Skip it and each one becomes its own guess, taken under pressure, in the middle of a sentence you are already halfway through.

examples.note: Une baguette now, la baguette next, de la baguette after that.
One decision, reused every time the word comes back.

recorded.desc: The un/une contrasts. Each pair in ONE TAKE, same voice, same speed, no pause longer than a beat: un armoire then une armoire, un table then une table, un escalier then une escalier. Across two takes the learner hears the difference between the recordings rather than between the articles. Do NOT over-articulate un: its vowel is nasal and no N is sounded, and a careful reading that lets the N through removes the only thing separating it from une.

The ten hero nouns, each said alone with a clear pause after it, ONE take straight through so the pace is even. Do not splice. Also supplies the preview table rows and the two word decks: le cahier, l’appartement, le ticket, le tableau, le fromage, la question, la voiture, une baguette, la cuisine, la chaise. « le ticket » and « une baguette » must come from the same take: they are the -et and -ette pair and the mission turns on hearing them side by side.

The elided nouns and the four listening lines. Read each noun naturally, WITHOUT separating the article from the word: the elision is meant to sound like one word, because that is why it hides what it hides. The listening lines are read straight through as whole sentences and again at 0.65 from the same take.

The second-hand shop scene. A neutral adult female voice for the dealer, unhurried and a little brisk, somebody closing up. The line « Une armoire ? Elle est au fond, à droite. » is the pivot: she is repeating the learner back with the article corrected, and it must sound like ordinary speech rather than a correction, because the whole point is that nobody tells you.
clipIds: Une armoire ? Elle est au fond, à droite.

recorded.desc: The four dictation sentences at natural pace, and again at 0.65 from the same take so the slow version is a slowing rather than a re-reading. Full stops audible; no exaggerated word separation, which would give the tile boundaries away. « L’ordinateur est sur le bureau. » must keep its elision joined.
clipIds: Vous ouvrez vos livres à la page dix.
Elle va lever la main pendant le cours.
Le professeur pose une question facile.

recorded.desc: The hardware shop exchange, shopkeeper lines only, warm and quick. « Une ampoule, oui. Pour quelle pièce ? » repeats the learner's own article back, so it has to sound like agreement rather than emphasis.
clipIds: Une ampoule, oui. Pour quelle pièce ?

segments.text: I am Camille. Today is gender, and specifically the part of it nobody measures for you.
You already know more French nouns than you can use, and the reason is the small word in front of each one.
Une armoire.
A wardrobe. You may know armoire. The une is the half that goes missing.
Learn the article, not the noun. That is the whole lesson, and here is why it is not obvious.
Le livre.
Book. It ends in e, and every course you have met says nouns ending in e are feminine. This one is not, and neither is about a third of them.
La table.
Table, feminine, same ending. Nothing on the page separates those two, so the rule is a lean and not a decision.
Now the endings that do work. Five of them point at un.
Le cahier. L’appartement. Le ticket. Le tableau. Le fromage.
Notebook, apartment, ticket, board, cheese. The endings are -ier, -ment, -et, -eau and -age.
And five point at une.
La question. La voiture. Une baguette. La cuisine. La chaise.
Question, car, baguette, kitchen, chair. The endings are -tion, -ure, -ette, -ine and -ise.
Every rule has something that breaks it, and the ones that break these are words you meet immediately.
L’eau. La peau.
Water and skin. Both feminine, and -eau points at masculine thirty-four times in thirty-seven. These are two of the three.
La page.
Page, feminine, against -age. Store an exception the same way you store anything else, which is with the article on it.
Your turn, with nothing in front of you. Ask for one baguette.
Now the cheese, and let the ending decide it for you.
And the hard one. Water, where the ending points the wrong way.
One question. I will say a noun and you tell me which article is hiding in it.
L’armoire.
La. Armoire is feminine, and nothing you heard said so, because le and la both shrink to l before a vowel.
Three things to keep. Learn the article, not the noun.
Ten endings do real work and cover about one noun in five. The famous one about a final e is right seven times in ten.
And when a noun turns up wearing l apostrophe, switch it to un or une in your head, because nothing else will ask.
À bientôt.

lessons.title: Les articles définis
lessons.intro: French has four ways to say the, and which one you need depends on the noun's gender, its number and the sound it starts with. The harder half is that English lets you use none of them and French never does.

say.text: Watch this happen. You know both words, you say both words, and the sentence still is not French.

beats.text: Lunch is finished and the plates are still on the table. Claire is filling the cafetière and asking everyone what they want.

beats.speaker: Claire
beats.fr: Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu aimes ?
beats.en: And you, what do you like?

beats.text: You have known the word for coffee since your first week. This is the easiest question anyone will ask you all afternoon.

options.en: the words you actually need
the same words, and one more

followUp.works: Right, and the extra word is not politeness or emphasis. French has no version of that sentence without it.
followUp.breaks: Every word there is a real French word, and the sentence is not French. Watch what Claire does next.

beats.speaker: Claire
beats.stage: She says it back to you with the word you left out, gently, the way you would to a child.

beats.heading: The word you left out
beats.body: Every word you said was a French word. The sentence was not, because English lets you drop the article in front of a general idea and French has no way to do that at all.
beats.coach: Nobody misunderstood you. They heard a learner.

beats.speaker: Claire
beats.fr: Le matin, le café. Le soir, le thé.
beats.en: Coffee in the morning. Tea in the evening.
beats.stage: Four nouns in one breath, and every one of them arrives with a word English would not have used.

beats.text: You were not misunderstood, and you were not corrected. You were repeated back to.

closing.text: When English says nothing, French says le. That is the decision, and you make it before you open your mouth.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: When English says nothing, French says le. By the end of this you will hear the gap before you fall into it.

goals.s: Put the article where English gives you nothing, which is where you currently lose the sentence.
Choose le, la, l apostrophe or les for any noun you know, in three questions.
Two of those three questions never ask what a1.03 taught you to store.
Tell l heure from le hibou, which is the only place the difference ever shows.

sections.title: Where English Says Nothing
sections.frSub: Là où l'anglais ne dit rien
sections.say: When English says nothing, French says le. Here is what that looks like in four sentences you would get wrong today.

cards.label: A thing in general
cards.head: Coffee, all coffee
cards.fr: Elle aime le café au lait.
cards.body: English says coffee. French says le café. The English sentence has nothing at all in front of the noun, and that empty slot is the whole problem, because there is no gap on the page for you to notice.

cards.label: A whole category
cards.head: Cats, meaning cats
cards.fr: Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
cards.sub: Cats love sleeping in the sun
cards.body: Not these cats. Cats as a species. English marks that by removing a word and French marks it by keeping one, which is the same idea running in opposite directions.

cards.label: A subject you study
cards.head: A language, a skill
cards.body: Languages, school subjects, sports and instruments all behave this way. Le français, les mathématiques, le tennis, le piano. English drops the word in front of every one of them.

cards.label: The other direction
cards.head: Where French drops it
cards.fr: Elle est infirmière et elle travaille la nuit.
cards.sub: She is a nurse and she works nights
cards.body: This one runs both ways in a single sentence. French refuses an article in front of a job after être, where English insists on one, and then adds la in front of a time where English gives nothing. a1.11 owns the first half.

cards.label: What le stands for
cards.head: One line, four words
cards.body: When English says nothing, French says le. Le there is shorthand for whichever of the four the noun actually takes. Working out which is the next act, and it is the easy half.

sections.title: The Rule In Twelve Lines
sections.say: Read the English first, then the French. Every English line is missing a word the French line has.

examples.note: A language. English has nothing in front of it and French has le.
Feminine, so la. The English still has nothing.
Plural in French, singular in English, and only French marks it at all.
An activity. Same shape, same missing word.
Sports take the article every time, and English never gives them one.
A type of food rather than particular plates on a table.
Preferring a kind of thing is the most common place this catches people.

examples.fr: Je préfère le sport en équipe.
examples.note: English plural, French singular, and the article arrives anyway.

examples.fr: Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
examples.en: Cats love sleeping in the sun.
examples.note: A whole species as the subject of the sentence.

examples.fr: Les abricots sont chers cette semaine.
examples.note: Apricots as a thing you buy, not the ones in your bag.

examples.fr: Les oiseaux volent vers le sud en hiver.
examples.note: Birds in general. Two articles here, and English has neither.

examples.fr: Le sport rend les enfants plus forts.
examples.note: Two bare nouns in the English and two articles in the French, in one short line.

sections.title: Le, La, L' and Les
sections.say: Four cards, one form each. This is the part you will have from a single reading, and it is the smaller half of the lesson.

cards.label: Masculine singular
cards.head: le
cards.body: For a masculine noun that starts on a consonant sound. This is the form the corpus shows you most: nearly eight hundred entries in this app begin with it, which is why it feels like the default even though it is one of four.

cards.label: Feminine singular
cards.head: la
cards.body: For a feminine noun that starts on a consonant sound. Nothing in the word maison tells you it is feminine, which is a1.03's whole subject and the reason you were asked to store the article with the noun.

cards.label: Before a vowel sound
cards.head: l'
cards.body: Le and la both shorten to this in front of a vowel sound, and the two become one word. Water is feminine and the card no longer says so, which is exactly the concealment a1.03 warned about.

cards.label: Any plural
cards.head: les
cards.body: Put those two in the plural and both take les. The sun is masculine and the moon is feminine for no reason anyone can give you, and les is the one form that never asks.

sections.title: Three Questions In Order
sections.say: Three questions, and you stop at the first one that answers yes. Two of the three never ask about gender.
steps: Is the noun plural? Then it is les, whatever its gender. You are done, and you never had to know whether it was masculine or feminine.
Does the noun start on a vowel sound? Then it is l apostrophe, whatever its gender. Done again, and again the gender never came up.
Neither? Then it is le or la, and only now do you need the gender you stored in a1.03. This is the one branch of the three that asks.

sections.title: The Grid, Row By Row
sections.say: The same four forms as a table. Tap any row for the case it covers and the one it does not.

detail.title: le
detail.body: The third question, masculine answer. You reach this row only after the noun turned out to be singular and to start on a consonant sound, which is why the gender matters here and nowhere else.

detail.title: la
detail.body: The third question, feminine answer. The same row as le with the other answer, and the only thing separating them is a fact about the noun that you cannot see on the page.

detail.title: l'
detail.body: The second question. School is feminine and the card will not tell you, because la and le both arrive here as the same two letters. Store it as une école the moment you meet it.

detail.title: les
detail.body: The first question, and the shortest route through. Masculine, feminine or a mixture, it makes no difference. The S on the end of the noun is usually silent, so les is the only part a listener hears carrying the plural.

sections.title: When Les Takes Over
sections.say: One form, and it is the only place in the language where the gender you worked to store is simply not consulted.

cards.label: Masculine plural
cards.head: les
cards.body: Masculine, and it takes les. Nothing about the article records that, and nothing later will ask you to.

cards.label: Feminine plural
cards.head: les again
cards.body: Feminine, and it takes exactly the same word. Put those two cards side by side and there is no way to tell which is which, which is the point of this mission.

cards.label: The one you hear
cards.head: Where the plural lives
cards.body: The S on the end of a French noun is usually silent, so les is doing all the work out loud. Drop it and a listener hears one friend. Nothing else in the phrase corrects that.

sections.title: Plurals, Both Genders
sections.say: Two decks. The line under each word is the gender it is hiding, and les is identical on both sides.

sections.title: Hearing The Plural
sections.say: Nothing on screen to work it out from. Listen for what happens at the join between the two words.

lines.fr: les livres
lines.en: the books

lines.fr: les amis
lines.en: the friends

lines.fr: les parents
lines.en: the parents

lines.fr: les enfants
lines.en: the children

questions.q: In « les livres », how many separate sounds do you hear before the noun?
opts: The noun starts with a Z
questions.why: Livres starts on a consonant, so les ends and livres begins. Two words, two starts, nothing joining them.

questions.q: In « les amis », what do you hear between the two words?
questions.why: Amis starts on a vowel, so the silent S of les wakes up as a Z and is said with the noun rather than with the article.

questions.q: You hear a Z at the join. What does that tell you about the noun?
opts: It starts on a vowel sound
questions.why: Only a vowel sound pulls that Z out. It says nothing about gender, because les never did.

sections.title: When Le And La Vanish
sections.say: Two forms collapse into one, and the thing they were carrying goes with them.

cards.label: Both become one
cards.head: le and la, gone
cards.body: The flat is masculine and the school is feminine, and in front of a vowel sound both articles shorten to the same two letters. The words are now indistinguishable and the gender is still there, unrecorded.

cards.label: Sound, not letter
cards.head: What counts as a vowel
cards.body: This is about the SOUND the noun starts on, not the letter it is spelled with. Heure begins with an h on the page and with a vowel in the mouth, so it shortens. The next mission is where that bites.

cards.label: The habit
cards.head: Convert it as it arrives
cards.body: a1.03 asked you to switch a new l apostrophe noun to un or une in your head before storing it. This is where that pays: oil is feminine, you will need la for it eventually, and nothing on this card says so.

sections.title: The Letter H, Two Ways
sections.say: Same letter, two behaviours, and no rule joining them. These are two lists to recognise, not a pattern to work out.

sections.title: Which H Is It?
sections.say: The bare noun on the front. Say the whole thing, article included, before you flip it.

sections.title: Three Traps
sections.say: Three, and the first one is the one you will make today.

errors.wrong: « J'aime café »
errors.right: « J'aime le café »
errors.why: When English says nothing, French says le. English lets a general noun stand bare and French does not, so this is not a missing flourish, it is a missing part of the sentence.

errors.wrong: « le eau »
errors.right: « l'eau »
errors.why: Two vowel sounds cannot sit next to each other here, so the e of le drops out and the two words join. This is not optional and there is no version of French that says le eau.

errors.wrong: « les ami »
errors.right: « les amis »
errors.why: The S of the noun is silent, so les is carrying the plural alone. Say it in front of a vowel and the S of LES comes back as a Z, joined onto the noun.

sections.title: Flip And Recall
sections.say: English on the front, and it gives you no article at all. Supply the French one before you flip.

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Six sentences, built from word tiles, and some of the tiles do not belong. The article is a tile like any other, so you have to place it.

sections.title: Say The Whole Thing
sections.say: Sixteen nouns, and none of them is a word on its own. Say the article and the noun as one piece.

sections.title: Six Moments This Week
sections.say: Six real moments, and in five of them English would have given you nothing to say.

Saying what you are learning
Turning down a whole food group
Asking where something is
Ordering the thing on the counter
Asking for the bill

sections.title: Your Turn At The Counter
sections.say: A café in the middle of the afternoon. Every line you say has an article in it, and one of them is the one you would drop.
sections.setting: A café counter in Bordeaux, mid-afternoon.

turns.ai: Bonjour ! Qu'est-ce que je vous sers ?
turns.en: Hello! What can I get you?
turns.user: Bonjour. Le café au lait, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: Hello. The café au lait, please.

alts.fr: Bonjour. Le thé, s'il vous plaît.
Bonjour, je prends le café au lait.
alts.en: Hello, I'll have the café au lait.

turns.ai: Et avec ça ? Nous avons des tartes.
turns.en: Anything with that? We have tarts.
turns.user: Non merci. Je n'aime pas les tartes.
turns.userEn: No thank you. I don't like tarts.

alts.fr: Non merci, je préfère les croissants.
alts.en: No thank you, I prefer croissants.

turns.ai: Très bien. Vous êtes en vacances ?
turns.en: Very good. Are you on holiday?
turns.userEn: No, I'm learning French here.

alts.en: Yes, I like the city a lot.

turns.ai: Ah, bravo ! C'est difficile, le français.
turns.en: Ah, well done! French is hard.
turns.userEn: Yes, but I love the language.

alts.fr: C'est vrai, mais j'adore le français.
alts.en: That's true, but I love French.

turns.ai: Voilà votre café. L'addition est sur la table.
turns.en: Here is your coffee. The bill is on the table.
turns.userEn: Thank you very much.

alts.en: Thank you! Have a good day.

sections.title: The Flat Above The Bakery
sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Tap any word you do not know, and notice how few nouns arrive on their own.
sections.text: Marc has just moved into a flat above a bakery in Toulouse, and his neighbour Sylvie has come up with two cups. She wants to know how he is settling in. « Alors, l'appartement te plaît ? » He says it is small, and then he says the part he actually likes. « Oui, beaucoup. La cuisine est petite, mais j'aime la lumière. » Sylvie points at the floor and grins, because everyone in the building asks this eventually. « Et le pain ? Tu entends le boulanger à quatre heures ? » He admits that he does, every single morning. « Je l'entends. Mais j'aime le pain, alors ça va. » She asks whether he has met anyone on the stairs yet. « Tu connais les voisins ? » He has met the two from the third floor and nobody else. « Les voisins du troisième, oui. Ils sont gentils. » Sylvie stands up to leave and gives him the one piece of advice that matters in this building. « Une chose. L'été, ouvre les fenêtres tôt. Après huit heures, il fait trop chaud. »

glossary.note: Masculine, and the card refuses to say so. Store it as un appartement, the way a1.03 asked.
The baker is masculine and the shop downstairs is la boulangerie, which is feminine. Nobody can tell you why.
Plural, so les, and the gender never entered into it.
The passage says l'été. The noun on its own is été, and the article in front of it is the word an English speaker would not have said at all.
Feminine and plural. Les does not care which, which is the whole of that mission in two words.

questions.q: What does Marc like about the flat, and what does he not?
questions.a: He likes the light. The kitchen is small.

questions.q: In « j'aime le pain », why is there a word there that English would not have?
questions.a: Because it means bread in general, and French keeps the article where English drops it.

questions.q: The passage says l'été. What is the noun on its own, and what is its gender?
questions.a: The noun is été, and it is masculine. The article hides that.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.back: J'aime le café. English gives you nothing; French needs le.
Is it plural? If yes, les, and stop.
Does it start on a vowel sound? If yes, l apostrophe.
Only now, le or la, and only now do you need the gender.
Two of them. les always, and l apostrophe in the singular.
l'heure. The h behaves like a vowel.
le hibou. The same letter, behaving like a consonant.
les haricots verts. Plural, so les settles it either way.

cards.front: Cats love sleeping in the sun.
cards.back: Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
cards.say: Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.

cards.front: What does the S in les do before a vowel?
cards.back: It comes back as a Z and joins onto the noun.
le soleil et la lune. Arbitrary, opposite, and worth storing together.
Elle est infirmière. Here French drops what English keeps.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have put the article where English gave you nothing, worked the three questions in order, and found the one letter that behaves two ways. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Four rounds. Most of these ask you to write the answer rather than pick it, because picking was never the hard part.

rounds.label: The missing word
rounds.say: The half of this lesson that is not about which article. It is about whether there is one.

questions.q: Write in French: I like coffee.
questions.why: When English says nothing, French says le. Coffee in general still takes le, and without it this is not a sentence.

questions.q: Fix this: « Nous aimons français. »
questions.why: A language is a general idea, so French keeps the article. English drops it, which is why the gap is invisible.

questions.q: Cats love sleeping in the sun. What does the French sentence start with?
questions.why: Cats as a species is the general case. French marks that by keeping a word where English removes one.

questions.q: Write in French: I am learning French.
questions.why: School subjects, languages, sports and instruments all take the article, and English gives none of them one.

questions.q: Fix this: « Elle aime musique. »
questions.why: Music is feminine, so la, but the reason a word is needed at all has nothing to do with gender.

questions.q: English says "Sport makes children stronger". How many articles does the French have?
questions.why: Le sport and les enfants. Both nouns are general, and English happens to mark neither of them.

rounds.label: Le or la
rounds.say: The third question, and the only one of the three that needs the gender.

questions.q: Maison is feminine. Write "the house".
questions.why: Feminine, singular, and it starts on a consonant sound, so you reach the third question and answer it with la.

questions.q: You need the gender of a noun in order to choose:
questions.why: Les and l apostrophe both settle it without asking. Only the third branch needs the gender.

questions.q: Livre is masculine. Write "the book".
questions.why: Masculine, singular, consonant sound. The one branch of the three where what a1.03 taught you is doing the work.

questions.q: Fix this: « le maison »
questions.why: Nothing in the word maison says it is feminine. That is why the article is stored with it.

questions.q: Lune is feminine and soleil is masculine. Write "the sun and the moon".
questions.why: Two everyday things with opposite genders and no reason behind either. This pair is worth storing as one card.

rounds.label: When gender stops counting
rounds.say: Two branches, and neither of them asks you a thing about the noun's gender.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: The Z at the join gives it away. It appears only when the noun starts on a vowel sound.

questions.q: Toilettes is feminine and plural. Write "the toilet".
questions.why: Plural, so the first question already answered it and the gender was never consulted.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Livres starts on a consonant, so the two words stay apart and there is no Z. Le livre would be one word shorter.

questions.q: École is feminine. Which is right?
questions.why: A vowel sound follows, so la shortens and the gender goes invisible before you needed it.

questions.q: Eau is feminine. Write "the water".
questions.why: La cannot sit in front of a vowel sound, so it shortens. There is no French that says la eau.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: One word, not two. Heure starts on a vowel sound despite the h, so the article shortens and joins onto it.

rounds.label: The two kinds of h
rounds.say: A closed list, not a rule. The article is the only place the difference is ever visible.

questions.q: Write "the owl". Hibou is masculine.
questions.why: This h behaves like a consonant, so le stays whole. Nothing on the page distinguishes it from the other kind.

questions.q: Both hôtel and hibou start with h. Why does only one take l apostrophe?
opts: There is no rule; the two are separate lists
questions.why: The split is a leftover of where the words came from. It is two lists, and gender is not in it.

questions.q: Fix this: « le heure »
questions.why: Heure behaves like a vowel, so the article shortens. Store the pair together and you never have to work it out.

questions.q: Write "the green beans".
questions.why: It is plural, so the first question settles it and the h never gets a chance to matter.

questions.q: Say it out loud: I like coffee.
questions.why: When English says nothing, French says le. If you said three words, the missing one is this lesson.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Six things, and one that a later lesson finishes for you.
sections.body: You can pick the right article for any noun you know, in three questions, and two of those three never ask you about gender. More usefully, you can hear the place where English gave you nothing and French wants a word, which is the error that marks a beginner more reliably than any accent does.
points: When English says nothing, French says le. Say it to yourself before a general noun and you will stop losing the sentence.
Plural takes les, whatever the gender. A vowel sound takes l apostrophe, whatever the gender.
Only le and la need the gender, which makes it one branch of three rather than the whole decision.
Every French h is silent, and only the article ever tells you which kind you are holding.
Store the noun with its article, the way a1.03 asked. This lesson is where that habit gets paid.
The Z you heard in les amis is a system of its own, and the sons track has a whole lesson on it.
du, au and aux are these same articles wearing a disguise. a1.29 takes them apart.

grammarAssumed: Every noun carries a gender, and it is stored with the noun rather than derived from it
The indefinite articles un and une, as the form gender is stored in
grammarIntroduced: The definite articles le, la, l apostrophe and les, and the order of the three questions that choose between them
The definite article in front of a general noun, where English uses no article at all
Nouns beginning with h splitting into two groups, distinguishable only by the article they take

overview.introFr: Le français a quatre façons de dire the, selon le genre, le nombre et le son du nom. Le plus dur, c'est que l'anglais peut n'en mettre aucun et le français jamais.

acts.title: The word English leaves out
acts.milestone: You have seen the mistake you cannot see from inside English.

acts.title: Which one to reach for
acts.milestone: Four forms, and three questions that pick between them.

acts.title: Where gender stops counting
acts.milestone: Les settles the plural without ever asking about gender.

acts.title: The sound, and the letter that lies
acts.milestone: You can tell l heure from le hibou, which nothing else in the language will tell you.

acts.title: Banked, and used

lessons.reframe: When English says nothing, French says le.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves a general noun bare, the way English does: J'aime café, Les chats becomes Chats, Le français becomes Français.
Reaches the third question and answers it with the wrong gender: le maison, la livre.
Keeps le or la where the noun is plural or starts on a vowel sound: le eau, la école, le parents.
Guesses at an h word rather than recognising which list it is on: l'hibou, le heure.

drills.title: The word that is not there
drills.coach: Read the English. It has nothing in front of the noun. Say the French, which does.
pairs: Cats love sleeping in the sun.
Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
Les oiseaux volent vers le sud en hiver.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: English says "I like tea". The French is:
drills.why: Tea in general takes le. J'aime un thé would mean one particular cup, which is not what the English said.

drills.title: Which one is it?
drills.coach: Nothing in the word tells you. This is the fact you stored in a1.03, being asked for.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Table is feminine. You want "the table".
drills.why: Feminine, singular, starts on a consonant sound, so the third question applies and the answer is la.

drills.title: Plural, vowel, or neither
drills.coach: Ask them in order. Plural first, vowel sound second, and only then reach for the gender.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A noun is feminine, singular, and starts on a vowel sound. Which article?
drills.why: The second question fired before the third one could. A vowel sound takes l apostrophe whatever the gender is.

drills.title: Two lists, one letter
drills.coach: There is nothing to work out here. Either you have stored it with its article or you have not.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these keeps its article whole?
drills.why: Le hibou. Heure and homme both behave like vowels and take l apostrophe, and only the article ever shows you the difference.

sheets.title: The four forms, on one screen

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Read the table by column rather than by row and the lesson falls out of it. The right-hand column is one word twice, and the bottom row is one word twice, so five of the six cells are settled before gender is mentioned. Only the top two cells of the left-hand column need it, which is why the three questions are asked in the order they are: plural first, vowel sound second, gender last and only if the first two came back no. Most textbooks draw this as a two by two grid with gender along the top, which puts the one thing you cannot see on the page in charge of a decision that usually does not need it.

sheets.title: The h words, both lists
contains: The h that lets the article shorten

rows.v: the hotel. Behaves like a vowel.
the hour. Behaves like a vowel.
history. Behaves like a vowel.
the oil. Behaves like a vowel.
the clock. Behaves like a vowel.
the man. Behaves like a vowel.
the hospital. Behaves like a vowel.
the habit. Behaves like a vowel.
the owl. Behaves like a consonant.
the hamster. Behaves like a consonant.
hockey. Behaves like a consonant.
the lobster. Behaves like a consonant.
the hip. Behaves like a consonant.
chance. Behaves like a consonant.
the hero. Behaves like a consonant.
the green beans. Consonant, and plural anyway.

sections.title: Why there is no rule
sections.body: Every h in French is silent, so nothing you can hear in the noun itself separates these two columns. The split is historical: one group came into French from Latin, where the h had already stopped being pronounced, and the other arrived later from Germanic and Frankish words where it still was. That h is gone now too, but the behaviour it left behind is not, and no feature of the modern spelling records it. So this is a list, and the reason it is a short and manageable list is that the second group is small. The practical consequence is the one this lesson keeps returning to: the article is the only place the difference is ever visible, so a noun stored on its own has thrown the fact away. Store le hibou, not hibou.

zero.title: Why the mistake is invisible from the inside
zero.body: English has three ways to introduce a noun and French has two. Where English says "the coffee" French says le café, and both languages agree. Where English says "a coffee" French says un café, and they agree again. But where English says plain "coffee", meaning coffee in general, French has no matching form: it still says le café. That third English option is the one with no French equivalent, and because it is the option an English speaker reaches for without thinking, the gap never announces itself. Nothing feels missing. The sentence simply is not French.

examples.note: We like French. Four words in English, four in French, and one of them has no English counterpart at all.
Cats in general. English marks the general case by removing a word; French marks it by keeping one.

pick.title: The order that saves you the gender
pick.body: There are four forms and three questions, asked in this order. Is the noun plural? Then it is les, and the gender does not enter into it. Does it start with a vowel sound? Then it is l apostrophe, and again the gender does not enter into it. Only when both answers are no does the third question arrive, and only then do you need to know whether the noun is masculine or feminine. Most courses present this as a two by two grid, which puts gender first and makes it look like the thing every choice depends on. In practice two of the three branches never reach it.

examples.note: Plural, so the first question already answered it.
A vowel sound, so the second one did.
Neither, so this is the one where the gender is finally needed.

plural.title: The form that ignores the question a1.03 taught you to ask
plural.body: Les is the plural for everything. Masculine, feminine, mixed, it makes no difference, and this is the one place in the language where the gender you worked to store is simply not consulted. It is also the form you will have met least: this app teaches nouns in the singular almost everywhere, so les gets a fraction of the exposure le does, and a learner can finish several lessons having barely seen it. Worth knowing too that the S on the end of the noun is usually silent, so les is the only part of the phrase a listener hears carrying the plural.

examples.note: Feminine, and it takes les like everything else.
Masculine, and it takes exactly the same word.

vowelSound.title: Not a vowel letter, which is where the shipped rule was wrong
vowelSound.body: Le and la both shorten to l apostrophe in front of a noun that STARTS ON A VOWEL SOUND. The distinction between sound and letter looks pedantic and costs a learner a whole category of nouns, because the letter h is written and never pronounced, so whether it counts depends on the word and not on the spelling. l heure and le hibou are both spelled with an h and only one of them shortens. a1.03 taught you that l apostrophe conceals the gender and that you should convert it to un or une before storing it. This lesson is the other half: how to know it was coming.

examples.note: A vowel letter and a vowel sound, so it shortens.
An h on the page, a vowel sound in the mouth, so it shortens too.
The same letter, and it does not shorten. Nothing on the page says why.

hSplit.title: A closed list to recognise, not a rule to work out
hSplit.body: Every French h is silent. What splits them is whether the word behaves as though it begins with a vowel or as though it begins with a consonant, and there is no rule that predicts which: the two groups are a leftover of where the words came from. So this is learned as two lists rather than derived, and the good news is that the article is the only place the difference is ever visible. A learner who has stored le hibou has stored the whole fact, and one who stored hibou on its own has stored nothing they can use.

examples.note: Behaves like a vowel.
Behaves like a consonant, and keeps la in full.
Plural and consonant-behaving, and les is unbothered by either.

storeIt.title: The habit a1.03 started, and what this lesson adds to it
storeIt.body: a1.03 asked you to store every noun with un or une in front of it, because the gender is not recoverable from the word. Keep doing that. What this lesson adds is that the definite article is where the storage gets tested: it is the form you reach for most, it is the one the h words only reveal themselves in, and it is the one English will keep tempting you to leave out. Nearly every noun in this app already carries an article in its own entry, so a card showing you the bare word has quietly taught you to store it bare.

examples.note: Stored the way you will need it.
And its opposite number, whose gender is just as arbitrary.

recorded.desc: The central contrast: « J'aime café » then « J'aime le café », in that order, one voice, one speed, ONE TAKE. The wrong version must be read at the same natural pace as the right one and not slowed or flagged, because the whole point is that it sounds almost fine. Do NOT over-articulate le; it is a schwa and it should half disappear, which is exactly why learners leave it out.

The four forms on their example nouns: le fromage, la maison, l'eau, les parents, then le livre, la table, l'école. ONE TAKE straight through so the pace is even and the four articles are directly comparable. le and la differ by one unstressed vowel and across two takes that difference is not audible.

The plural pairs, each pair in ONE TAKE: les livres then les amis, les parents then les enfants. The join is the entire teaching, so les amis must be said as one piece at natural speed and never separated into two words for clarity. Also supplies the listening mission.

l'appartement, l'école, l'heure, l'huile, and for contrast le appartement is NOT to be recorded: there is no such thing and a clip of it would be teaching a form that does not exist. One take, natural pace, and the article and noun joined as a single word throughout.

The two h lists as PAIRS, one take per pair, so each contrast is comparable: l'heure then le hibou, l'hôtel then le hockey, l'homme then le homard, l'huile then la hanche. Every h is silent in all of them, so nothing should be aspirated; the difference the learner is listening for is whether the article joins on or stands alone.

The twelve example sentences, each read straight through at natural conversational pace and again at 0.65 from the same take. Never assembled from separately recorded words: the article runs into the noun and that join is what the mission is showing.
clipIds: Je préfère le sport en équipe.
Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
Les abricots sont chers cette semaine.
Les oiseaux volent vers le sud en hiver.
Le sport rend les enfants plus forts.

recorded.desc: The kitchen scene. A warm adult female voice for Claire, unhurried and friendly rather than corrective: the line « Ah, tu aimes le café. » is the pivot of the whole lesson and it must not sound like a telling-off. She is repeating it back, not marking it wrong. « Le matin, le café. Le soir, le thé. » is four articles in one breath and should be said at full speed, so they are as small as they really are.

Le matin, le café. Le soir, le thé.

recorded.desc: The three traps, wrong then right for each, ONE TAKE per pair: « J'aime café » then « J'aime le café », « le eau » then « l'eau », « les ami » then « les amis ». The wrong readings must be spoken naturally rather than mangled, because the point is that a learner cannot hear their own error.

The six dictation sentences at natural pace, and again at 0.65 from the same take so the slow version is a slowing rather than a re-reading. No exaggerated word separation, which would give the tile boundaries away, and specifically no pause after the article: the learner has to hear that les chats is two words without being handed the gap.

Les enfants adorent le sport collectif.
