errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong row of the table: avez for nous, avons for vous, ont for il.
Uses être where French uses avoir: Je suis faim, Je suis froid, Tu es raison. The error the reframe exists to kill.
Gives an age with être, or gives a bare number with no ans behind it.
Drops the de after besoin or envie, or the à after mal, because the other eleven carry nothing.
Says il a chaud about the weather, or je suis chaud about themselves. One noun, two wrong verbs.
Writes pas de faim, or drops the de from pas de voiture. The rule applied one noun too far, or not far enough.
Reads every j'ai as a possession, including the 23% of them that are a past tense.

drills.title: Pronoun in, form out
drills.coach: The pronoun is on the left. Say the form out loud before you turn the card, and join it up where it joins.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You and one colleague have an appointment. Which form?
drills.why: nous takes avons. avez belongs to vous, and the two are the pair most often swapped because both bind to their pronoun.

drills.title: Have it, do not be it
drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right out loud, and notice which verb you reached for first.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You have not eaten since breakfast. What do you say?
drills.why: Faim is hunger, a thing, so it is had rather than been. The English am in front of hungry is what makes the wrong one feel right.

drills.title: A number of years, held
drills.coach: Every line here is a real age sentence. Say each one out loud and listen for the two things that are never missing: the verb, and the word ans.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: She is forty. Which is right?
drills.why: The verb is avoir and the word ans is never dropped. The third option gives a number with nothing to count, which is not an age in French.

drills.title: What comes after it?
drills.coach: Three buckets and eleven of the fourteen belong in the last one. Put each line where the word after the expression tells you it goes.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You need a pen. Which is right?
drills.why: Besoin always carries de, and de shortens in front of a vowel sound. Mal is the one that takes à, and the other eleven take nothing at all.

drills.title: The person, or the room?
drills.coach: Read each one and ask who is warm. If it is somebody, the verb is avoir. If it is the day, the verb is neither of the two you have learned.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: The weather is warm today. Which is right?
drills.why: The weather takes neither of this lesson's verbs. Il a chaud would say that a particular man is too warm, which is a sentence about a person.

drills.title: What does the no leave behind?
drills.coach: Say the negative out loud before you flip. Half of these leave a de behind and half of them leave nothing.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one is right for "I am not hungry"?
drills.why: Faim never had an article, so the negative had nothing to collapse to de. The de only appears where a un, une or des had to be removed.

drills.title: Having, or something else?
drills.coach: Read the word straight after the form of avoir. A noun means somebody has something. Another verb means a past tense, and nothing is owned.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one is NOT about having something?
opts: J'ai perdu mes clés ce matin.
drills.why: Perdu is a verb and it sits directly after the form of avoir, so the pair is a past tense. Nothing is being owned in that sentence.

sheets.title: avoir, in full
contains: All nine pronouns with their form

sections.title: The full paradigm
rows: they have, any group with a man in it

sections.title: The four that join up
sections.body: Four of the six start on a vowel, and every one of them pulls the silent consonant in front of it back to life. Nous ends in a silent s and avons starts on an a, so the s returns as a z and the two words are said as one: noo-za-VOHⁿ. The same happens with vous avez, ils ont and elles ont. Je is the fifth case and it behaves differently: rather than binding, it disappears, because ai starts on a vowel and je loses its e and is written j apostrophe. Only tu as and il a stand apart with nothing joining them, and those two happen to be the pair that sound identical, since the s of as is silent. So the six forms produce five distinct sounds, and the pronoun is what tells you which of the two identical ones you are hearing. That is why French never drops a subject pronoun the way English drops one in a list.

sections.title: Against être, which you already have
sections.body: These are the two most used verbs in French and they are the two most broken, for the same reason: a form said a hundred times a day is never smoothed out by analogy the way a rare verb is. You have now learned both outright and no other verb will ask this of you again. One pair is worth keeping apart from the start because it belongs to both lessons at once: ils sont opens on a clear s and means they are, while ils ont carries a z over from the silent s of ils and means they have. Slowed down they are obvious. At conversational speed the z against the s is the only thing separating them, and there is no other clue in the sentence, because both are followed by whatever comes next with no pause. The written forms are further apart than the spoken ones, so reading them will not train your ear. That is what the listening mission is for.

sheets.title: The fourteen, and the two rules around them

sections.title: The four places English points the wrong way

rows.v: J'ai vingt ans, never Je suis vingt ans. And ans is never left off.
J'ai faim, J'ai froid, J'ai peur. Eleven of them, all the same swap.
Il fait chaud for the room. J'ai chaud for the person.
besoin de, envie de, mal à. The other eleven carry nothing.
Je n'ai pas de voiture. The une collapsed to de.
Je n'ai pas faim. Nothing collapsed, because nothing was there.

sections.title: The sentences where it stops meaning have
sections.body: Across the a1 corpus, 119 of the 522 rows that open on a form of avoir are not about having anything, which is 23 out of every hundred. J ai perdu mes clés is I lost my keys. Elle a pris le bus is she took the bus. Nous avons réservé une table is we booked a table, and the table belongs to a restaurant. In every one of them the form of avoir is doing a job you have not been taught yet, and the word straight after it is what gives it away: one noun means somebody has something, another verb means a past tense. The reason this matters now rather than later is that you will read four or five times as much French as you produce for the next year, and a learner who meets j ai only as I have will read almost a quarter of what they meet as a possession that is not there. You are not being asked to use this. You are being asked to see it and move on.

haveNotBe.title: The swap English makes you get wrong
haveNotBe.body: English puts "am" in front of hungry, cold, afraid, right and twenty. French puts "have" in front of all five, and the word after it is a thing rather than a description: hunger, cold, fear, reason, years. So the sentence is not built the way yours is, and translating it word by word gives you something that is not French at all. This is the single most audible beginner error there is, because it lands in the first sentence anyone says about themselves.

examples.note: Hunger, had. Not hungry, been.
Twenty years, had. Je suis vingt ans is not a sentence.

ageRule.title: Years are something you have
ageRule.body: An age in French is a number of years that belong to you, so it takes avoir and the word ans is never left off. You already own every number you need for this: they were the whole of three earlier lessons, and nothing about counting changes here. What changes is the frame the number sits in, and there is exactly one of them. Ask it with quel âge and answer it with a form of avoir plus a number plus ans.

examples.note: The number is the part you already had.
The question that gets you the answer, in the tu form.

sixForms.term: ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont
sixForms.title: Six forms, and three of them join up out loud
sixForms.body: Nine pronouns sit behind six forms, which is the arithmetic you were given two lessons ago and which holds here unchanged. What is new is that four of the six start on a vowel, so the pronoun in front binds to them: nous avons is said as one word with a Z in the middle, and so are vous avez, ils ont and elles ont. That join is not optional and it is the thing that separates ils ont from ils sont.

examples.note: noo-za-VOHⁿ, one word out loud.
eel-ZOHⁿ. The S of ils wakes up, exactly as it did in vous êtes.

withComplement.term: besoin de, envie de, mal à
withComplement.title: The three that behave differently
withComplement.body: Eleven of these expressions are a straight swap of have for be. These three are not: they land on need, want and hurt rather than on be, and all three carry a little word after them that has to come too. Besoin and envie take de, which shortens to d apostrophe in front of a vowel. Mal takes à, and then the à joins whatever article the body part wants: au dos, à la tête, aux dents. Learn them as a group of three and the other eleven stay simple.

examples.note: need, and the de that has to come with it.
hurt, and the à that merged with le to make au.

pastAmbush.term: j'ai in front of a verb
pastAmbush.title: When have stops meaning have
pastAmbush.body: Nearly a quarter of the sentences in this course that open on a form of avoir are not about having anything. J ai perdu mes clés is I lost my keys, not I have lost-keys. When the word after the form of avoir is another verb, the pair is a past tense and the have has gone. You are not learning that tense yet. What you need now is to recognise it on sight, so that a sentence you meet in the wild does not get read as a possession that is not there.

examples.note: Lost, in the past. There is no having in this sentence.
A real possession, for comparison. One noun after the form, no second verb.

noArticleUnderNo.term: pas de, and pas on its own
noArticleUnderNo.title: Two ways a negative can land
noArticleUnderNo.body: Say no to a thing you could count and the word in front of it collapses to de: j ai une voiture becomes je n ai pas de voiture. Say no to one of these expressions and nothing collapses, because there was never an article there to lose: j ai faim becomes je n ai pas faim. Both halves are on the same screen for a reason. Which one you get tells you which kind of sentence you were in, and it is the whole of what the negation unit will ask you to do.

examples.note: une became de. The rule you met on un, une and des.
Nothing to collapse, so nothing collapsed. Never pas de faim.

recorded.desc: THE SIX FORMS AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, IN PARADIGM ORDER, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED. Six forms recorded in six sessions are six performances, and the learner is trying to hear a SET: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between them teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read the bare forms first, then the six full sentences in the same take. THE FOUR LIAISONS ARE THE POINT AND THEY ARE NOT OPTIONAL: nous avons, vous avez and ils ont are each ONE phonetic word with a z in the middle, and the slow take must be that join stretched rather than the join taken apart. A learner who hears them separated once will produce them separated forever. Do not sound the s of as, the t of ont, or the final s of ils.

recorded.desc: The two minimal pairs this lesson turns on, EACH PAIR RECORDED BACK TO BACK IN ONE TAKE by the same voice at the same speed, in the way sons.07 pins rec-h-pairs and a1.11 pins rec-a1-11-pairs. ils ont against ils sont is a liaison z against an s and it is the same take or it is nothing: recorded apart, the learner compares two performances instead of two verbs. il a against ils ont is a liaison that exists against one that does not, and the temptation is to lean on the ils to make it clearer. DO NOT. The whole difficulty is that nobody leans on it in speech. Then the four listening lines at natural pace and again at 0.65.

recorded.desc: The scene break and the swap deck. « Je suis vingt ans. » must be read PLAINLY and at ordinary pace, not comically and not hesitantly: the entire teaching of the scene is that it sounds like a normal sentence right up until it stops, and any performance signalling that it is wrong destroys that. Then « J'ai vingt ans. » in the same take at the same pace, so the only audible difference is the verb. Run the verb straight into the number with no pause, because a gap there is exactly where a learner inserts être.

The eleven expressions as ONE TAKE in the order the drill shows them, one voice, one speed, no teaching pause between them. The learner is being shown that eleven separate things are one thing, and eleven separately recorded clips would teach eleven separate things. Keep the nasals closed: faim ends on a nasal vowel with NO m sound, raison ends on a nasal vowel with NO n sound, and honte likewise. Those three are the ones a reader will over-articulate.

The four English-speaker traps, wrong form then right form, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears the difference rather than a correction. Je suis vingt ans / J'ai vingt ans. Je suis faim / J'ai faim. Je suis chaud / J'ai chaud. Je n'ai pas de faim / Je n'ai pas faim. Read every wrong version plainly rather than comically: two of these four are real French sentences that mean something else, and a performance that marks them as errors removes the reason they are dangerous.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of one woman in her seventies at an ordinary kitchen-table pace. The beat where she asks again (« Pardon ? Vous avez quel âge ? ») must be patient and unbothered rather than corrective or impatient: the whole point of the scene is that she is not correcting anybody, she simply did not receive a sentence, so any edge on it turns the moment into a telling-off and the teaching is lost.

items.ipa: sə vjø tʁɛ̃ ʁu.lɛ a pɛn a ka.ʁɑ̃t ki.lɔ.mɛtʁ a lœʁ

items.fr: Sur mon téléphone, j'ai deux cents photos de nos vacances.
items.en: On my phone, I have two hundred photos of our vacation.
items.ipa: syʁ mɔ̃ te.le.fɔn ʒe dø sɑ̃ fɔ.to də no va.kɑ̃s

items.fr: Depuis mille huit cent quarante, ce moulin tourne sans arrêt.
items.en: Since eighteen forty, this mill has turned without stopping.
items.ipa: də.pɥi mil ɥi sɑ̃ ka.ʁɑ̃t sə mu.lɛ̃ tuʁn sɑ̃.z a.ʁɛ
items.notes: "Mille" is always invariable, it never takes an s.

items.fr: Notre classe compte dix-neuf filles et huit garçons.
items.en: Our class has nineteen girls and eight boys.
items.ipa: nɔtʁ klas kɔ̃t diz.nœf fij e ɥi gaʁ.sɔ̃
items.notes: Compound numbers below one hundred take hyphens between their parts, except around "et".

items.fr: Chaque année, ce port accueille cent bateaux de pêche.
items.en: Every year, this harbor welcomes a hundred fishing boats.
items.ipa: ʃak a.ne sə pɔʁ a.kœj sɑ̃ ba.to də pɛʃ
items.notes: "Cent" is invariable here since it is not a round multiple of a hundred used alone.

items.fr: En trois mois, elle a économisé cent cinquante euros.
items.en: In three months, she saved one hundred fifty euros.
items.ipa: ɑ̃ tʁwa mwa ɛl a e.kɔ.no.mi.ze sɑ̃ sɛ̃.kɑ̃t ø.ʁo

items.fr: Cet arbre majestueux mesure vingt mètres de hauteur.
items.en: This majestic tree is twenty meters tall.
items.ipa: sɛ.t aʁbʁ ma.ʒɛs.tɥø mə.zyʁ vɛ̃ mɛtʁ də o.tœʁ

items.fr: Jusqu'au sommet, on a compté quarante-quatre marches.
items.en: To the top, we counted forty-four steps.
items.ipa: ʒys.ko sɔ.mɛ ɔ̃.n a kɔ̃.te ka.ʁɑ̃t katʁ maʁʃ
items.notes: Compound numbers below one hundred take hyphens between their parts, except around "et".

items.fr: Ce fermier possède soixante vaches dans son champ.
items.en: This farmer owns sixty cows in his field.
items.ipa: sə fɛʁ.mje pɔ.sɛd swa.sɑ̃t vaʃ dɑ̃ sɔ̃ ʃɑ̃

items.fr: En juin, ma grand-mère fête ses soixante-quinze ans.
items.en: In June, my grandmother celebrates her seventy-fifth birthday.
items.ipa: ɑ̃ ʒɥɛ̃ ma ɡʁɑ̃.mɛʁ fɛt se swa.sɑ̃t kɛ̃z ɑ̃
items.notes: Numbers from soixante-dix to soixante-dix-neuf are built on "soixante", not a separate word for seventy.

items.fr: Ce vieux cinéma propose des places à sept euros cinquante.
items.en: This old cinema offers seats for seven euros fifty.
items.ipa: sə vjø si.ne.ma pʁɔ.poz de plas a sɛ.t ø.ʁo sɛ̃.kɑ̃t
items.notes: The number liaises with the following vowel-initial word, adding a consonant sound that is not written.

items.fr: Ce bâtiment ancien a été rénové en deux mille dix.
items.en: This old building was renovated in two thousand ten.
items.ipa: sə ba.ti.mɑ̃ ɑ̃.sjɛ̃ a e.te ʁe.nɔ.ve ɑ̃ dø mil dis

items.fr: Pour ce stylo, j'ai payé quatre-vingt-dix-neuf centimes.
items.en: For this pen, I paid ninety-nine cents.
items.ipa: puʁ sə sti.lo ʒe pe.je ka.tʁə.vɛ̃ dis nœf sɑ̃.tim

items.fr: Ce marin a navigué pendant cinquante ans.
items.en: This sailor sailed for fifty years.
items.ipa: sə ma.ʁɛ̃ a na.vi.ge pɑ̃.dɑ̃ sɛ̃.kɑ̃t ɑ̃

items.fr: En dix-neuf cent vingt-quatre, ce stade a été construit.
items.en: In nineteen twenty-four, this stadium was built.
items.ipa: ɑ̃ diz.nœf sɑ̃ vɛ̃t katʁ sə stad a e.te kɔ̃s.tʁɥi
items.notes: Compound numbers below one hundred take hyphens between their parts, except around "et".

items.fr: Depuis le début de l'année, elle a lu douze livres.
items.en: Since the beginning of the year, she has read twelve books.
items.ipa: də.pɥi lə de.by də la.ne ɛl a ly duz livʁ

items.fr: Depuis vingt-huit ans, ce facteur distribue le courrier.
items.en: For twenty-eight years, this mailman has delivered mail.
items.ipa: də.pɥi vɛ̃t ɥi.t ɑ̃ sə fak.tœʁ dis.tʁi.by lə ku.ʁje
items.notes: The final "t" of "huit" is pronounced here because of the liaison with the next word.

items.fr: Pour ce soir, il faut au moins quarante chaises.
items.en: For tonight, we need at least forty chairs.
items.ipa: puʁ sə swaʁ il fo o mwɛ̃ ka.ʁɑ̃t ʃɛz

items.fr: Pour huit mille euros, ce pêcheur a vendu son bateau.
items.en: For eight thousand euros, this fisherman sold his boat.
items.ipa: puʁ ɥi mil ø.ʁo sə pɛ.ʃœʁ a vɑ̃.dy sɔ̃ ba.to

items.fr: Chaque semaine, la bibliothécaire range plus de cinq cents livres.
items.en: Every week, the librarian shelves more than five hundred books.
items.ipa: ʃak sə.mɛn la bi.bli.jɔ.te.kɛʁ ʁɑ̃ʒ plys də sɛ̃k sɑ̃ livʁ

items.fr: Dans la même banque, ce comptable a travaillé trente-neuf ans.
items.en: At the same bank, this accountant worked thirty-nine years.
items.ipa: dɑ̃ la mɛm bɑ̃k sə kɔ̃.tabl a tʁa.va.je tʁɑ̃t nœf ɑ̃

items.fr: Trois buts à zéro, voilà le score final du match.
items.en: Three goals to nil, that is the final score of the match.
items.ipa: tʁwa by a ze.ʁo vwa.la lə skɔʁ fi.nal dy matʃ

items.fr: Ce notaire a rédigé plus de mille contrats.
items.en: This notary drafted more than a thousand contracts.
items.ipa: sə nɔ.tɛʁ a ʁe.di.ʒe plys də mil kɔ̃.tʁa
items.notes: "Mille" is always invariable, it never takes an s.

items.fr: Pour deux cent cinquante euros, elle a acheté cette bague.
items.en: For two hundred fifty euros, she bought this ring.
items.ipa: puʁ dø sɑ̃ sɛ̃.kɑ̃t ø.ʁo ɛl a aʃ.te sɛt bag
items.notes: "Cent" is invariable here since it is not a round multiple of a hundred used alone.

items.fr: Ce gardien surveille le parc depuis vingt-deux ans.
items.en: This caretaker has watched over the park for twenty-two years.
items.ipa: sə gaʁ.djɛ̃ syʁ.vɛj lə paʁk də.pɥi vɛ̃t dø.z ɑ̃
items.notes: "Deux" liaises with the next word as a z sound.

items.fr: Pour quatre nuits, nous avons réservé deux chambres.
items.en: For four nights, we booked two rooms.
items.ipa: puʁ ka.tʁə nɥi nu.z a.vɔ̃ ʁe.zɛʁ.ve dø ʃɑ̃bʁ

items.fr: Depuis quarante-cinq ans, ce menuisier fabrique des tables.
items.en: For forty-five years, this carpenter has been making tables.
items.ipa: də.pɥi ka.ʁɑ̃t sɛ̃k ɑ̃ sə mə.nɥi.zje fa.bʁik de tabl

items.fr: Dans la rue, j'ai trouvé un billet de cinquante euros.
items.en: In the street, I found a fifty-euro bill.
items.ipa: dɑ̃ la ʁy ʒe tʁu.ve œ̃ bi.jɛ də sɛ̃.kɑ̃t ø.ʁo

items.fr: Au total, ce château compte cent trois pièces.
items.en: In total, this castle has one hundred three rooms.
items.ipa: o tɔ.tal sə ʃa.to kɔ̃t sɑ̃ tʁwa pjɛs

items.fr: À l'aéroport, on a attendu plus de trois heures.
items.en: At the airport, we waited more than three hours.
items.ipa: a la.e.ʁo.pɔʁ ɔ̃.n a a.tɑ̃.dy plys də tʁwa.z œʁ
items.notes: "Trois" liaises with the next word as a z sound.

items.fr: En cinquante-cinq minutes, elle a couru dix kilomètres.
items.en: In fifty-five minutes, she ran ten kilometers.
items.ipa: ɑ̃ sɛ̃.kɑ̃t sɛ̃k mi.nyt ɛl a ku.ʁy di ki.lɔ.mɛtʁ
items.notes: The final "x" of "dix" is silent before the consonant "kilomètres".

items.fr: Chaque automne, ce verger produit encore quatre cents kilos de pommes.
items.en: Every autumn, this orchard still produces four hundred kilos of apples.
items.ipa: ʃak o.tɔn sə vɛʁ.ʒe pʁɔ.dɥi ɑ̃.kɔʁ ka.tʁə sɑ̃ ki.lo də pɔm

items.fr: Pendant notre voyage, nous avons visité vingt et une villes.
items.en: During our trip, we visited twenty-one cities.
items.ipa: pɑ̃.dɑ̃ nɔtʁ vwa.jaʒ nu.z a.vɔ̃ vi.zi.te vɛ̃.t e yn vil
items.notes: "Une" agrees with the feminine "villes", giving "vingt et une" instead of "vingt et un".

items.fr: Pour le mariage, j'ai commandé cent cinquante invitations.
items.en: For the wedding, I ordered one hundred fifty invitations.
items.ipa: puʁ lə ma.ʁjaʒ ʒe kɔ.mɑ̃.de sɑ̃ sɛ̃.kɑ̃t ɛ̃.vi.ta.sjɔ̃
items.notes: "Cent" is invariable here since it is not a round multiple of a hundred used alone.

items.fr: Ce professeur a formé plus de deux mille étudiants.
items.en: This professor has trained more than two thousand students.
items.ipa: sə pʁɔ.fɛ.sœʁ a fɔʁ.me plys də dø mi.l e.ty.djɑ̃

items.fr: Pour le dîner, nous avons dépensé quatre-vingt-quinze euros.
items.en: For dinner, we spent ninety-five euros.
items.ipa: puʁ lə di.ne nu.z a.vɔ̃ de.pɑ̃.se ka.tʁə.vɛ̃ kɛ̃z ø.ʁo

items.fr: Cette année, le village fête ses huit cents ans d'existence.
items.en: This year, the village is celebrating its eight hundredth anniversary.
items.ipa: sɛt a.ne lə vi.laʒ fɛt se ɥi sɑ̃.z ɑ̃ dɛg.zis.tɑ̃s
items.notes: "Cents" takes an s here as a round multiple of a hundred with no smaller number following.

items.fr: mettre les clés dans le sac
items.en: to put the keys in the bag
items.respell: mehtr lay KLAY dahn luh SAHK

items.fr: ranger les assiettes dans le placard
items.en: to put the plates away in the cupboard
items.respell: rahn-ZHAY lay zah-SYEHT dahn luh plah-KAHR

items.fr: brancher la lampe dans la prise
items.en: to plug the lamp into the socket
items.respell: brahn-SHAY lah LAHNP dahn lah PREEZ

items.en: to hang a painting on the wall

items.fr: poser le vase sur la table
items.en: to put the vase on the table
items.respell: poh-ZAY luh VAHZ sür lah TAHBL

items.en: to pour water into the kettle
to put clothes away in the wardrobe

items.fr: chercher ses affaires sous le lit
items.en: to look for one's things under the bed
items.respell: shehr-SHAY say zah-FEHR soo luh LEE

items.fr: allumer la radio avant de partir
items.en: to turn on the radio before leaving
items.respell: ah-lü-MAY lah rah-DYOH ah-vahn duh par-TEER

items.fr: éteindre le four après la cuisson
items.en: to turn off the oven after cooking
items.respell: ay-TIHNDR luh FOOR ah-preh lah kwee-SOHN

items.fr: mettre une pièce dans la machine
items.en: to put a coin in the machine
items.respell: mehtr ün PYEHS dahn lah mah-SHEEN

items.en: to slip a letter into the envelope

items.fr: attacher la ceinture avant de conduire
items.en: to fasten the belt before driving
items.respell: ah-tah-SHAY lah sihn-TÜR ah-vahn duh kohn-DWEER

items.fr: ranger les outils dans la boîte
items.en: to put the tools away in the box
items.respell: rahn-ZHAY lay zoo-TEE dahn lah BWAHT

items.fr: brancher le chargeur avant de dormir
items.en: to plug in the charger before sleeping
items.respell: brahn-SHAY luh shar-ZHUR ah-vahn duh dor-MEER

items.fr: Le café est chaud, fais attention.
items.en: The coffee is hot, be careful.
items.notes: “est” (from être) and “ai” sound alike here, but only “est” fits after “le café”.

items.fr: Notre maison a un grand jardin.
items.en: Our house has a big garden.
items.ipa: nɔtʁ mɛ.zɔ̃ a œ̃ ɡʁɑ̃ ʒaʁ.dɛ̃
items.notes: “a” (from avoir) has no accent, unlike “à” (to/at).

items.fr: Elle se réveille tôt et elle se lève sans bruit.
items.en: She wakes up early and gets up quietly.
items.ipa: ɛl sə ʁe.vɛj to e ɛl sə lɛv sɑ̃ bʁɥi
items.notes: “tôt” has a circumflex; it is not the same word as “taux”.

items.fr: Les élèves écoutent attentivement la maîtresse.
items.en: The students listen attentively to the teacher.
items.notes: “maîtresse” keeps the circumflex from “maître”, even with the feminine ending.

items.en: He plays soccer with his friends on weekends.

items.en: She goes swimming three times a week.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Elle fait de la natation","t":"she goes swimming"},{"w":"trois fois","t":"three times"},{"w":"par semaine.","t":"a week"}]}

items.fr: Ça fait longtemps qu'on ne s'est pas vus.
items.en: It's been a long time since we've seen each other.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Ça fait longtemps","t":"it's been a long time"},{"w":"qu'on","t":"that we"},{"w":"ne s'est pas vus.","t":"haven't seen each other"}]}

items.en: My parents have lived in the countryside for ten years.

items.en: She broke her arm falling off her bike.

items.en: Children learn to read from the age of six.

items.fr: Elle vient d'obtenir un nouveau poste dans son entreprise.
items.en: She just got a new position at her company.

items.en: She has had a bruise on her arm since yesterday.

items.fr: Il vaut mieux prendre le métro pour éviter les embouteillages.
items.en: It's better to take the subway to avoid traffic jams.

items.fr: Le panda se nourrit presque uniquement de bambou.
items.en: The panda feeds almost exclusively on bamboo.
items.notes: {"tiles":[{"w":"Le panda","t":"the panda"},{"w":"se nourrit","t":"feeds"},{"w":"presque uniquement","t":"almost exclusively"},{"w":"de bambou.","t":"on bamboo"}]}

items.fr: Il faut qu'elle organise mieux ses journées si elle veut tout finir.
items.en: She needs to organize her days better if she wants to finish everything.
items.ipa: il fo kɛl ɔʁ.ɡa.niz mjø se ʒuʁ.ne si ɛl vø tu fi.niʁ
items.notes: “Il faut que” requires the subjunctive “organise”.

items.fr: Je prends un café noir le matin.
items.en: I have a black coffee in the morning.
items.ipa: ʒə pʁɑ̃ œ̃ ka.fe nwaʁ lə ma.tɛ̃
items.notes: The final letters of “prends” are silent, even though they're written.

items.fr: Elle a commandé un café allongé sans sucre.
items.en: She ordered a long black coffee without sugar.
items.ipa: ɛl a kɔ.mɑ̃.de œ̃ ka.fe a.lɔ̃.ʒe sɑ̃ sykʁ
items.notes: “Commandé” ends in é because it follows “a” in the passé composé.

items.fr: Nous buvons notre café sur la terrasse quand il fait beau.
items.en: We drink our coffee on the terrace when the weather's nice.
items.ipa: nu by.vɔ̃ nɔtʁ ka.fe syʁ la tɛ.ʁas kɑ̃.t‿il fɛ bo
items.notes: “Quand il” is linked by a liaison, pronounced “kɑ̃.t‿il”.

items.fr: Ce café reste bondé bien qu'il y ait moins de touristes cet été.
items.en: This café stays packed even though there are fewer tourists this summer.
items.ipa: sə ka.fe ʁɛst bɔ̃.de bjɛ̃ kil j‿ɛ mwɛ̃ də tu.ʁist sɛ.t‿e.te
items.notes: “Ait”, the subjunctive of avoir, sounds like “est” but is spelled differently after “bien que”.

items.fr: C'est le seul café du quartier où l'on peut encore fumer en terrasse.
items.en: It's the only café in the neighborhood where you can still smoke on the terrace.
items.ipa: sɛ lə sœl ka.fe dy kaʁ.tje u lɔ̃ pø ɑ̃.kɔʁ fy.me ɑ̃ tɛ.ʁas
items.notes: “Où l'on” uses the elided “l'” before “on” for a smoother sound.

items.fr: La maison est grande et blanche.
items.en: The house is big and white.
items.ipa: la mɛ.zɔ̃ ɛ ɡʁɑ̃d e blɑ̃ʃ
items.notes: “Grande” and “blanche” take the feminine ending to agree with “maison”.

items.fr: Nous avons repeint les volets en vert cet été.
items.en: We repainted the shutters green this summer.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ ʁə.pɛ̃ le vɔ.lɛ ɑ̃ vɛʁ sɛ.t‿e.te
items.notes: “Repeint” stays invariable even though “volets” is plural, since the object follows the verb.

items.fr: Le grenier est plein de vieux cartons poussiéreux.
items.en: The attic is full of old, dusty boxes.
items.ipa: lə ɡʁə.nje ɛ plɛ̃ də vjø kaʁ.tɔ̃ pu.sje.ʁø
items.notes: The final “x” of “vieux” is silent.

items.fr: Ils ont fait construire une véranda derrière la maison.
items.en: They had a veranda built behind the house.
items.ipa: il.z‿ɔ̃ fɛ kɔ̃s.tʁɥiʁ yn ve.ʁɑ̃.da dɛ.ʁjɛʁ la mɛ.zɔ̃
items.notes: “Fait” stays invariable in this causative construction with “construire”.

items.fr: La maison qu'ils ont achetée a besoin de gros travaux.
items.en: The house they bought needs major renovations.
items.ipa: la mɛ.zɔ̃ ki.l‿ɔ̃.t‿a.ʃə.te a bə.zwɛ̃ də ɡʁo tʁa.vo
items.notes: “Achetée” agrees in the feminine with “maison”, the preceding direct object.

items.fr: Je me lève à sept heures tous les jours.
items.en: I get up at seven every day.
items.ipa: ʒə mə lɛv a sɛ.t‿œʁ tu le ʒuʁ
items.notes: “Lève” takes an accent grave because the stem vowel is stressed, unlike in “lever”.

items.fr: D'habitude, je me douche avant de prendre mon petit-déjeuner.
items.en: I usually shower before having breakfast.
items.ipa: da.by.tyd ʒə mə duʃ a.vɑ̃ də pʁɑ̃dʁ mɔ̃ pə.ti de.ʒœ.ne
items.notes: “D'habitude” elides “de” before the vowel of “habitude”.

items.fr: Le soir, ils regardent les informations avant de se coucher.
items.en: In the evening, they watch the news before going to bed.
items.ipa: lə swaʁ il ʁə.ɡaʁd le.z‿ɛ̃.fɔʁ.ma.sjɔ̃ a.vɑ̃ də sə ku.ʃe
items.notes: “Informations” is almost always used in the plural in French, unlike its English equivalent.

items.fr: Depuis qu'elle travaille de nuit, ses horaires ont complètement changé.
items.en: Since she started working nights, her schedule has changed completely.
items.ipa: də.pɥi kɛl tʁa.vaj də nɥi se.z‿ɔ.ʁɛʁ ɔ̃ kɔ̃.plɛt.mɑ̃ ʃɑ̃.ʒe
items.notes: “Ses horaires” is plural, so it takes “ses” rather than the singular “son”.

items.fr: Elle fait de la natation trois fois par semaine.
items.en: She goes swimming three times a week.
items.ipa: ɛl fɛ də la na.ta.sjɔ̃ tʁwa fwa paʁ sə.mɛn
items.notes: “Fois” is invariable and never takes an s, even after “trois”.

items.fr: Nous avons couru un marathon l'année dernière.
items.en: We ran a marathon last year.
items.ipa: nu.z‿a.vɔ̃ ku.ʁy œ̃ ma.ʁa.tɔ̃ la.ne dɛʁ.njɛʁ
items.notes: “Couru” is the irregular past participle of “courir”, not “couri”.

items.fr: Bien qu'elle se soit entraînée tous les jours, elle n'a pas gagné la course.
items.en: Even though she trained every day, she didn't win the race.
items.ipa: bjɛ̃.kɛl sə swa.t‿ɑ̃.tʁɛ.ne tu le ʒuʁ ɛl na pa ɡa.ɲe la kuʁs
items.notes: “Entraînée” agrees with the feminine subject because the reflexive pronoun acts as the object.

items.fr: Les randonneurs se sont perdus dans le brouillard pendant deux heures.
items.en: The hikers got lost in the fog for two hours.
items.ipa: le ʁɑ̃.dɔ.nœʁ sə sɔ̃ pɛʁ.dy dɑ̃ lə bʁu.jaʁ pɑ̃.dɑ̃ dø.z‿œʁ
items.notes: “Perdus” takes the masculine plural ending to agree with “les randonneurs”.
